Infants learning a tonal language such as Yoruba reliably separate words that differ only in pitch during their first year, whereas infants learning English attend to those same pitch distinctions only briefly before losing them. ____, the sound contrasts a baby must hear in order to acquire the language around it are the contrasts that baby's perception keeps.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: even so | as a result | in other words | for example
explanation: C is correct; the second sentence recasts the comparison as a general principle about what perception retains, so it says the first sentence over again in different terms. A wrongly asserts concession, but the general statement does not oppose the observation. B treats the principle as an effect produced by the infant data; the sentence is an interpretation, not a consequence of it. D claims exemplification, yet no new instance is introduced; the same finding is simply rephrased.

question:
When a planet crosses the face of its star, the depth of the dip in brightness tells researchers how large the planet is compared with the star. ____, tracking how the star's own light shifts toward red and then blue over the same orbit reveals how strongly the planet pulls on it, which is how the planet's mass is worked out.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: as a result | specifically | in addition | in contrast
explanation: C is correct; two independent measurement techniques are listed, one yielding size and one yielding mass, so the transition should mark that a further item is being added. A wrongly asserts that the velocity measurement is caused by the brightness dip, though the two are separate observations. B claims the second narrows to a particular case of the first, but mass is a different quantity from size, not a finer view of it. D signals opposition between the methods, which the sentences give no support for.

question:
A stand of winter rye sown after a maize harvest takes up the nitrogen left in the soil and holds it in its tissues instead of letting the nutrient wash into streams. ____, crimson clover sown late in the same season likewise captures residual nitrogen through the winter and returns it to the topsoil when the plants are turned under in spring.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: as a result | likewise | even so | in other words
explanation: B is correct; two different cover crops are shown doing the same job by the same kind of mechanism, so the transition should mark parallel case with parallel effect. A wrongly asserts that clover's behaviour results from rye's; one crop does not cause the other to work. C implies the clover sentence runs against the rye sentence, when the two agree. D treats the clover clause as a restatement of the rye clause, but a second species is genuinely new information rather than the same claim reworded.

question:
After wolves returned to Yellowstone, elk spent less time grazing in the stream valleys, and the willows and aspens there grew taller than they had during the 1990s. ____, beaver colonies have spread along several of those same valleys, since beavers need tall willows both to cut for lodges and to eat.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: therefore | even so | by contrast | in other words
explanation: A is correct; taller willows are stated in the first sentence and beavers, which require them, expand in the second, so the second follows from the first. B wrongly asserts concession, as if growing beaver numbers contradicted the recovering willows when the sentence supplies the reason for the increase. C claims the beaver case opposes the elk case, though the two form one chain. D treats the beaver sentence as a rephrasing of the vegetation sentence, but a new species and a new trend are introduced.

question:
Bus rapid transit keeps vehicles moving by handling fare payment before the bus arrives, a design choice that matters most on routes where large numbers of passengers board and leave at every stop. ____, the TransMilenio system in Bogotá places prepayment kiosks and raised boarding platforms at its stations, so a bus can dwell for seconds instead of the several minutes a curbside route needs.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: by contrast | as a result | for example | in other words
explanation: C is correct; the first sentence states a general design principle and the second names one real system built on it, so the transition must introduce an instance. A wrongly asserts contrast, treating Bogotá's system as opposing the principle it actually illustrates. B claims the specific system results from the principle as though the description itself produced it, whereas the sentence's job is to exhibit the principle at work. D treats the Bogotá details as a rephrasing of the general claim, but a named network with its own figures is an example rather than an equivalent statement.

question:
Cholera spreads through water contaminated with infected waste, so cases cluster around a shared pump, well, or pipeline rather than passing directly between the households next to one another. ____, response teams confronting an outbreak put their effort into repairing the water system and raising chlorine levels instead of isolating the families who have fallen ill.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: even so | in contrast | for the same reason | accordingly
explanation: D is correct; the first sentence supplies a fact about how the disease travels, and the second describes action taken on the strength of that fact, so the transition must signal action taken in line with that reasoning. A wrongly asserts concession, implying the response contradicts what is known about spread. B claims the two sentences describe opposing situations, when the response simply follows the science. C suggests both statements share one cause, but the second is a deliberate response to the first, not a parallel effect of it.

question:
X-ray tomography of the Antikythera mechanism has recovered Greek lettering hidden inside corrosion on bronze fragments that earlier catalogues listed simply as an illegible lump. ____, the calendar built into the surviving gearing still cannot be dated with confidence, because the year-starting conventions it might reflect differed from one Hellenistic city to another.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: as a result | nevertheless | in other words | moreover
explanation: B is correct; the lettering recovered in the first sentence raises expectations of a firm date, and the second sentence says a date remains uncertain, so a concessive transition marks the limits of the new information. A wrongly asserts consequence, as if improved imaging caused the dating problem; the problem persists despite the imaging. C treats unresolved dating as the same claim as recovered lettering reworded, which it is not. D presents the difficulty as an extra point in the same direction, whereas it runs against the progress just reported.

question:
During an El Niño year, the trade winds over the Pacific slacken, and warm surface water piles up in the central basin, lifting local sea level by several centimetres. ____, in the eastern basin the usual warm surface layer thins as cold water keeps rising from below, so sea level off the coast of Peru falls relative to normal.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: accordingly | in other words | meanwhile | moreover
explanation: C is correct; the two sentences describe simultaneous conditions in two different parts of one ocean, with opposite signatures, so a temporal transition is required. A wrongly asserts a cause-effect relation, as if the cold water off Peru were produced by the pooling of warm water in the centre, when both departures occur together as effects of the weakened winds. D claims the two trends add up in the same direction, but one basin rises while the other drops. B treats the eastern basin description as a restatement of the central one, which differs in location and in sign.

question:
A modern orchestra tunes to the note the oboe sounds, because that pitch is fixed by the spacing of the instrument's tone holes and can be given instantly at any rehearsal. ____, ensembles that play at the lower historical standard often have the leader of the first violins set the reference note instead, since the string instruments cannot be trimmed or reeded the way a wind instrument can.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: however | as a result | in other words | likewise
explanation: A is correct; the first sentence explains why the oboe leads tuning and the second says that in another kind of ensemble a string player does, so the transition must signal a difference. B wrongly asserts consequence, implying the violins' role is produced by the oboe's advantage; the reasoning is reversed by the second sentence's own cause. C claims the two sentences say the same thing, but they describe different practices. D asserts similarity of procedure, when the identity of the reference instrument changes.

question:
Lead white paint darkens where polluted air carries hydrogen sulfide, because the metal reacts to form brown lead sulfide inside the paint film. ____, conservators who clean discoloured lead-white passages often apply a dilute peroxide solution, which converts the sulfur compound back into white sulfate rather than scraping the layer away.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: as a result | by contrast | meanwhile | moreover
explanation: A is correct; the chemistry of darkening motivates the choice of cleaning agent, so the second sentence follows from the first. B wrongly asserts a contrast between the two facts, when the treatment is designed around the problem. C reframes the relationship as mere simultaneity, as if conservators just happen to use peroxide at the same time that lead sulfide forms. D treats the treatment as an added point rather than a consequence of the stated chemistry.

question:
Annual layers in glacier ice can be counted much like tree rings, and deep cores from Antarctica preserve more than 800,000 such yearly couplets. ____, where the moving ice has stretched the deeper couplets so thin that they blur together, researchers confirm their count against chemically distinctive ash from eruptions whose dates are independently established.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: in other words | indeed | for the same reason | as a result
explanation: B is correct; the second sentence strengthens and carries further the claim that layer counting works, by adding the corroboration used where counting is hardest, so a confirming transition is the best fit. A wrongly asserts restatement, but volcanic cross-checks are new information, not the counting claim reworded. C implies both facts arise from one cause, whereas the first concerns ice flow and the second concerns dating method. D claims confirmation follows as an effect from thinning layers, when it is a methodological response to a difficulty.

question:
The first coins struck in Lydia were made from electrum, a naturally occurring alloy whose mix of gold and silver varies from one batch to the next. ____, the standardized coinage later issued under King Croesus was struck from gold and silver that had each been refined separately, so its users could rely on an exact metal content.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: likewise | as a result | in other words | by contrast
explanation: D is correct; variable natural alloy is set against separately refined metal, so the transition must mark the difference between the two stages of coinage. A wrongly asserts similarity between the two issues, ignoring the change in how the metal was prepared. B claims Croesus's coinage is caused by the earlier electrum practice rather than differing from it. C treats the later coinage as a restatement of the earlier description, though the two differ in composition and guarantee.

question:
Once European printers worked with reusable metal type in the mid-fifteenth century, a single press could turn out copies of a text far faster than a house of scribes copying it by hand. ____, because a page could be taken apart and a mistaken line reset on its own, an error no longer meant ruling out the whole text again, which kept the price of a printed sheet steady from run to run.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: as a result | in other words | by contrast | in addition
explanation: D is correct; the first sentence credits movable type with speed and the second adds a distinct further advantage, the cheap correction of a single line, so the transition should mark an extra point. A wrongly asserts consequence, as if steady prices were produced by the output rate rather than by the separateness of the type. B treats the correction detail as the speed claim reworded, though it concerns a different cost. C signals opposition between two benefits that in fact reinforce one another.

question:
After a bite from an animal that might be rabid, a vaccine given even several days later can still protect the person, because the virus travels slowly along nerves toward the brain and the immune response has time to catch up. ____, that same slow progress is what justifies the ten-day watchful waiting applied to a dog that has bitten someone, since an animal still healthy at the end of that period cannot have been infectious on the day of the bite.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: nevertheless | in addition | for the same reason | in other words
explanation: C is correct; both the post-bite vaccination and the observation of the dog rest on one identical underlying fact, the leisurely pace at which the virus moves, which is what this transition points to. A wrongly asserts concession, although the second practice follows smoothly from the first rather than against it. B presents the observation period as a separate additional point, missing that its justification is the reason already given. D claims restatement, but the second sentence shifts subject to a monitored animal instead of rephrasing the first.

question:
Palynologists reconstruct the vegetation of a Holocene lake by counting the microscopic pollen grains that settled into its sediments year after year. ____, the ratio among tree-pollen types in one thin sediment band indicates which species made up the canopy standing around the water at that moment.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: by contrast | as a result | in other words | specifically
explanation: D is correct; the first sentence names a method in general and the second narrows to one measurement within that method, a pollen ratio in a single band, so a specifying transition is required. A wrongly asserts opposition between the two statements, which describe the same work at different levels of detail. B claims the ratio analysis is an effect of the general method rather than a particular step inside it. C treats the second sentence as an equivalent rephrasing, yet it supplies information the first withholds.

question:
In the history of English, a consonant sound lost at the start of a word can leave the neighbouring consonants to be pronounced as one cluster instead of a sequence, which is how the modern word yoke came to open with its present sound. ____, the shape of a word's beginning in contemporary English sometimes owes itself to a sound speakers no longer make.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: even so | in other words | for example | moreover
explanation: B is correct; the second sentence states in plainer, more general terms exactly what the historical account in the first sentence already claimed, so a restatement transition fits. A wrongly asserts concession, though the general statement does not qualify the specific one. C claims exemplification, but no fresh instance is offered; the yoke example is already inside the first sentence. D presents the second sentence as a further new point, when it carries no information beyond the first.

question:
Patients whose aphasia follows damage to Broca's area commonly omit small words such as is and the, producing brief sentences that researchers describe as agrammatic. ____, recordings of some of these patients capture them saying the word the without error inside phrases learned whole, such as thank the Lord, which suggests the difficulty lies in assembling new sentences rather than in storing the word.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: even so | for example | in other words | accordingly
explanation: A is correct; the expected reading of agrammatism is that these words are lost, and the recordings show one of them produced correctly, so the second sentence states something that holds despite the first. C wrongly asserts restatement, but the memorised-phrase finding is new evidence with an interpretation attached, not the same claim reworded. B inverts the relation, treating the recordings as illustrating the omission pattern they actually complicate. D asserts consequence, as if fluent retrieval in set phrases followed from the omission of function words.

question:
Before England's Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834, most parishes paid for relief out of a local rate levied on property, so a slump in wages forced a town to support its own out-of-work labourers from its own funds. ____, parishes with large manufacturing populations carried rates several times higher than rural parishes of comparable property values, a difference contemporaries complained about bitterly.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: however | in addition | for the same reason | therefore
explanation: D is correct; relief cost fell on the parish where unemployment occurred, so industrial parishes with many jobless workers carried heavier rates, meaning the second sentence follows from the first. A wrongly asserts a contrast, when the burden difference is the predictable result of the funding rule. B treats the disparity as a separate extra fact, missing the consequence relation. C claims both statements merely share a cause, but the first describes a system and the second describes what that system produced.

question:
After the price of crude oil climbed in 1973 and again in 1979, economies in Western Europe that imported most of their energy saw inflation spread through industry as fuel and freight costs rose. ____, in those same years the Gulf economies exporting the oil recorded large surpluses on their current accounts, as payments for each barrel flowed inward instead of outward.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: as a result | meanwhile | that said | in other words
explanation: B is correct; the sentences describe two developments occurring in the same period on opposite sides of the same price shock, so a temporal transition is what ties them. A wrongly asserts that European inflation caused the export surpluses, whereas both outcomes trace back to the higher price of oil. C implies the surplus sentence contradicts the inflation sentence, but the two are simply different effects. D claims restatement, yet the second sentence changes the actors, the region, and the direction of the money.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a forest nursery study of mycorrhizal networks.
* Seedlings of Douglas fir that were linked to neighboring plants by fungal threads gained about 28 percent more carbon than seedlings grown with their roots isolated.
* The fungal species involved cannot fix carbon through photosynthesis.
* Isotope tracing showed that the carbon reaching the seedlings had originated in the leaves of surrounding plants.
* Threads linking unrelated species were less common than threads linking plants of the same species.

The student wants to emphasize a contrast between the fungal partner's own ability to produce carbon and the carbon it delivered to the seedlings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Seedlings that were connected by fungal threads gained about 28 percent more carbon than seedlings whose roots were grown in isolation. | The fungal species involved cannot fix carbon through photosynthesis, and threads linking unrelated species were less common than threads linking plants of the same species. | Although the fungal partner cannot fix carbon through photosynthesis, the carbon it delivered to the seedlings had originated in the leaves of surrounding plants. | The fungal species involved cannot fix carbon through photosynthesis, yet it still grew threads that connected many seedlings to one another.
explanation: This item asks you to synthesize notes around one specified contrast: the fungus supplies carbon but manufactures none of its own. The third option joins those two facts with a concessive structure, so the contrast is exactly the one requested. The first option reports the measured gain instead of the contrast in carbon origins, the second adds the unrelatedness of cross-species threads, which has nothing to do with where the carbon came from, and the third pairs the fungus's inability with its thread formation, which is a different contrast from the one named in the goal.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about the standardization of intermodal freight containers.
* In 1956 a refitted tanker carried 58 purpose-built metal containers from Newark to Houston.
* Several carriers had already been using wooden boxes of assorted sizes for local freight.
* Major operators did not agree on a compatible lock-and-frame system for cranes and chassis until 1968.
* Between 1968 and 1977 the share of containerized cargo handled by early-adopting ports roughly tripled.

The student wants to describe the order in which the milestones in container standardization occurred. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The 1956 voyage demonstrated purpose-built metal containers, major operators agreed on a compatible lock-and-frame system in 1968, and the share of containerized cargo handled by early-adopting ports then roughly tripled between 1968 and 1977. | The 1956 voyage carried 58 metal containers from Newark to Houston, and the share of containerized cargo handled by early-adopting ports roughly tripled between 1968 and 1977. | Several carriers had been using wooden boxes of assorted sizes for local freight, and the tanker used for the 1956 voyage had been refitted rather than newly built. | There was a voyage carrying 58 metal containers in 1956, and there was an agreement among major operators on a compatible lock-and-frame system in 1968.
explanation: The goal is chronological, so the effective answer must place all three standardization milestones in sequence with explicit ordering. The first option does that and adds the consequence that follows the 1968 agreement. The second omits the 1968 agreement altogether, the third describes earlier wooden boxes and how the tanker was obtained, neither of which is a standardization milestone, and the fourth simply lists the two dates without any language showing which came first.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about nighttime temperatures in the districts of a city.
* Districts with more than 40 percent tree canopy recorded nighttime temperatures up to 3.1 degrees Celsius lower than nearby districts with little canopy.
* Leaves release water vapor, a process that removes heat from the surrounding air.
* Dense pavement and dark roofing store solar energy during the day and release it after sunset.
* The measurements were taken at 34 stations over eleven consecutive summer nights.

The student wants to explain why districts with little tree canopy remained warmer after sunset. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Districts with more than 40 percent canopy recorded nighttime temperatures up to 3.1 degrees Celsius lower than nearby districts with little canopy. | The measurements were taken at 34 stations over eleven consecutive summer nights, and districts with little canopy recorded the warmer nights. | Leaves release water vapor, which removes heat from the air, and dense pavement and dark roofing release the solar energy they stored once the sun has set. | Districts with little canopy lacked the cooling that leaves produce by releasing water vapor, and their dense pavement and dark roofing gave back after sunset the solar energy they had stored during the day.
explanation: To explain a cause, the answer has to connect the mechanisms in the notes to the warmer nights in the sparse-canopy districts. The last option does both halves: it removes the leaf cooling those districts lack and identifies the materials returning stored heat after sunset. The first option states the size of the temperature gap rather than its cause, the second offers the sampling design, which cannot explain anything, and the third describes the two mechanisms as general facts without attaching them to the districts in question.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a study of animal remains at a Neolithic village site.
* Researchers measured strontium isotope ratios in the tooth enamel of 61 sheep and goat teeth.
* Strontium ratios differ with the geology of the area where an animal formed its teeth.
* Enamel does not remodel after it forms, so its chemistry records an animal's early environment rather than the environment where it died.
* Twenty-two of the animals had ratios matching geology more than 90 kilometers from the site.

The student wants to explain how the researchers were able to determine where the animals had grown up. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Twenty-two of the animals analyzed at the site had strontium ratios matching geology more than 90 kilometers from the village. | Because enamel does not remodel after it forms, its strontium ratios preserve the geology of the place where an animal grew its teeth, allowing the researchers to read that origin from the 61 teeth they measured. | Strontium isotope ratios were measured in tooth enamel, and tooth enamel does not remodel once it has formed. | The researchers analyzed 61 teeth from the site, and twenty-two of those teeth came from animals whose ratios matched distant geology.
explanation: The goal asks for the reasoning behind a method, which requires the principle linking enamel chemistry to origin. The second option supplies that link, the permanence of enamel, and then shows how it was applied to the 61 teeth. The first and fourth options give the study's result rather than the procedure that produced it, and the third lists the two relevant facts side by side without explaining that ratios therefore record a place, which is the step that makes the method work.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about traffic on two suspension bridges.
* The Kestrel Point bridge recorded 1.8 million vehicle crossings in its first full year.
* The Wexler Narrows bridge recorded 2.46 million crossings in its first full year.
* The crossing charge at Wexler Narrows was 40 percent lower than the charge at Kestrel Point.
* The two bridges opened in the same calendar year.

The student wants to use the notes to compare the relationship between crossing charges and crossing volumes at the two bridges. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The Wexler Narrows bridge charged 40 percent less per crossing and still recorded 2.46 million crossings in its first full year, compared with 1.8 million at the higher-priced Kestrel Point bridge. | The Wexler Narrows bridge recorded 2.46 million crossings in its first full year, and the two bridges opened in the same calendar year. | The Kestrel Point bridge recorded 1.8 million crossings, and both bridges opened in the same year. | The Kestrel Point bridge recorded 1.8 million crossings in its first full year, and the Wexler Narrows bridge recorded 2.46 million in its first full year.
explanation: The goal requires both quantities, the charges and the volumes, set against each other. Only the first option does that, pairing the lower charge with the higher count for the same bridge. The second and third options mention only one volume and add the opening year, which is irrelevant to a charge-and-volume comparison, and the fourth gives both volumes correctly but never brings in the charges the goal asks about.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a survey of walking habits in one town.
* Researchers mailed questionnaires to 12,000 households and received 3,100 completed forms.
* Respondents reported an average of 41 minutes of walking per day.
* Questionnaires listed activities in the order in which respondents most often performed them.
* The completed forms came back between March and May.

The student wants to explain why the survey's figure of 41 minutes may not represent all households in the town. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Respondents reported an average of 41 minutes of walking per day, an estimate gathered with mailed questionnaires. | The questionnaires listed activities in the order respondents most often performed them, and the completed forms came back between March and May. | Only 3,100 of the 12,000 mailed questionnaires came back, so the reported average may describe the households that chose to respond rather than the town as a whole. | Researchers mailed questionnaires to 12,000 households, and 3,100 households returned completed forms between March and May.
explanation: The goal is to identify a threat to the estimate's representativeness, which means the answer must connect the low return rate to the possibility that respondents differ from nonrespondents. The third option makes exactly that connection. The first restates the estimate itself, the second describes the questionnaire layout and the return window, neither of which bears on representativeness, and the fourth supplies the same two sample figures the correct answer uses but never draws the consequence for the average.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a trial of winter cover crops.
* Plots sown with a legume cover crop yielded 12 percent less maize the following summer than unplanted plots.
* Legume cover crops are generally expected to raise the yield of the crop that follows them.
* A wet spring delayed the planting of the following maize crop by nineteen days.
* In this region, maize planted after the usual date consistently yields less than maize planted on time.

The student wants to account for the unexpected yield result in the cover crop trial. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Plots sown with the legume cover crop yielded 12 percent less maize than unplanted plots, even though legumes are generally expected to raise the yield of the crop that follows. | Although legume cover crops usually raise the yield of the next crop, a wet spring delayed maize planting by nineteen days, and maize planted late in this region consistently yields less, which is what produced the 12 percent deficit. | A wet spring delayed the planting of the following maize crop by nineteen days, and unplanted plots served as the comparison for the sown plots. | Legume cover crops are generally expected to raise the yield of the crop that follows them, and the trial recorded maize yields in the summer after the cover crop was terminated.
explanation: Accounting for a surprise requires three moves: name the expectation, name the factor that defied it, and show how that factor produced the outcome. The second option performs all three by routing the delay through the regional finding about late planting. The first merely restates that the result was unexpected, the third notes the delay and the presence of unplanted plots without linking them to the deficit, and the fourth gives the expectation and the trial's timing, which leaves the surprise entirely unexplained.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a city's decision to build bus rapid transit instead of a light rail line.
* The corridor's projected daily ridership was 34,000 boardings.
* A light rail line on the corridor was estimated to cost 2.3 billion and would have required a new tunnel segment.
* Bus rapid transit would run in the existing roadway and was estimated at 410 million.
* Planners had committed to opening a transit spine on the corridor before the next budget cycle.

The student wants to present the reasons planners chose bus rapid transit for this corridor. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The corridor's projected daily ridership was 34,000 boardings, and a light rail line there was estimated to cost 2.3 billion. | Planners had committed to opening a transit spine on the corridor before the next budget cycle, and the corridor's projected daily ridership was 34,000 boardings. | Bus rapid transit was estimated at 410 million, and a light rail line would have required a new tunnel segment on the corridor. | Because bus rapid transit could run in the existing roadway at an estimated 410 million rather than the 2.3 billion a light rail line needed with its new tunnel, it was the option that fit the deadline planners had already accepted for opening a spine.
explanation: A statement of reasons must show why the chosen option served the goal, so the answer has to tie the cost and right-of-way advantages to the commitment planners had made. The last option does that with explicit causal language. The first describes the corridor and one cost figure without mentioning the chosen option, the second gives the deadline and the ridership projection but no comparative reason, and the third lists a cost and an engineering fact about the two schemes without stating that these are what drove the decision.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a training program for distance runners.
* Runners who spent eighteen hours at altitude added 4.2 percent to their estimated hemoglobin mass.
* A control group training at the same mileage near sea level showed no measurable change.
* Both groups followed an identical six-week mileage schedule.
* Hemoglobin mass affects how much oxygen the blood can carry.

The student wants to describe the effect the altitude exposure had on the runners. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Both groups followed an identical six-week mileage schedule, and hemoglobin mass affects how much oxygen the blood can carry. | The altitude group spent eighteen hours above sea level, while the control group trained at the same mileage near sea level. | Runners who spent eighteen hours at altitude added 4.2 percent to estimated hemoglobin mass, whereas a control group covering the same mileage near sea level showed no measurable change. | Hemoglobin mass affects how much oxygen the blood can carry, and the altitude group's program lasted six weeks.
explanation: The goal asks for an effect, so the answer must report what changed in the altitude group relative to the comparison group. The third option gives the 4.2 percent gain and the control group's lack of change, which together are the full description of the effect. The first reports the training design and the physiology of hemoglobin, background facts that answer how the study was built or why hemoglobin matters, the second names both groups' conditions without reporting any outcome, and the fourth repeats the definition of hemoglobin along with the program's length.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a deep-sea survey of a mid-ocean ridge.
* A remotely operated vehicle filmed a vent field at 2,740 meters that no earlier report had described.
* The survey covered 60 kilometers of ridge across four dives.
* Tube worms were clustered around warm seepage rather than around the hottest openings.
* Earlier charts had placed active venting 120 kilometers farther north along the same ridge.

The student wants to explain why the survey's discovery was unexpected given what earlier charts showed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: A remotely operated vehicle filmed a previously undescribed vent field, and tube worms in that field were clustered around warm seepage. | The survey covered 60 kilometers of ridge across four dives, and earlier charts had placed active venting 120 kilometers farther north along the same ridge. | Earlier charts placed active venting 120 kilometers farther north along the ridge, so filming a new vent field at 2,740 meters put active venting a considerable distance from where those charts had indicated it. | Tube worms clustered around warm seepage rather than around the hottest openings, and the survey completed four dives along the ridge.
explanation: Explaining why a finding is unexpected requires setting the new observation against the prior expectation, which the third option does by joining the charts' northern placement to the newly filmed field. The first option pairs the discovery with the animals' positioning, a biological description that says nothing about the charts, the second lists the survey's extent and the chart location without noting that they conflict, and the fourth gives the tube worm distribution and the dive count, both irrelevant to the surprise.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about the first serialization of a Victorian novel.
* The novel appeared in twenty monthly parts during 1873 and 1874.
* Readers wrote to the publisher asking that one particular chapter be shortened.
* Sales of the closing part were about twice the sales of the opening part.
* The author restored two omitted scenes when the novel was issued in a single volume in 1875.

The student wants to describe how the novel's audience responded while the serialization was running. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The novel appeared in twenty monthly parts during 1873 and 1874, and the author restored two omitted scenes for the 1875 single-volume edition. | Sales of the closing part were about twice those of the opening part, and at least some readers intervened directly, writing to the publisher to ask that a chapter be shortened. | Readers wrote to the publisher asking that a particular chapter be shortened, and that chapter was one of the twenty monthly parts. | Sales of the closing part were about twice the sales of the opening part, and a single-volume edition appeared in 1875.
explanation: The goal concerns audience behavior during the run, so the answer should combine the purchasing trend with the direct intervention readers made. The second option supplies both acts of response. The first gives publication structure and a later editorial decision, neither of which is a reader response, the third pairs the letters with the format in which the novel was appearing, which restates the situation rather than the response to it, and the fourth attaches the sales growth to the publication year of the single volume, an irrelevant detail given that the 1875 edition postdates the run.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about nautical vocabulary in a landlocked dialect.
* The dialect contains eighteen nautical terms used figuratively, including several for being in difficulty.
* Traders carried coastal goods to the region's fairs between 1780 and 1840.
* The region's only earlier contact with seafarers came through a customs office abolished in 1702.
* Nine of the eighteen terms are first recorded in letters written in the 1820s.

The student wants to explain why the notes lend more support to one route of borrowing than to the other. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The dialect contains eighteen nautical terms used figuratively, and traders carried coastal goods to the region's fairs between 1780 and 1840. | Traders carried coastal goods to the region's fairs between 1780 and 1840, a period when the customs office was no longer operating. | Nine of the eighteen terms are first recorded in letters from the 1820s, and those eighteen terms are used figuratively rather than as sailing instructions. | Because nine of the eighteen terms are first recorded in letters from the 1820s, their appearance fits the period of fair trade between 1780 and 1840 far better than it fits contact through a customs office abolished in 1702.
explanation: Choosing between two explanations takes the evidence that discriminates them, here the date of first attestation, plus a reason why that date suits one contact route and not the other. The fourth option supplies all three parts. The first reports the terms and the fair trade without ever weighing the two routes against each other, the second notes only that the office had closed, which establishes timing without the attestation evidence, and the third gives the attestation date alongside the terms' figurative use, a combination that says nothing about where the words came from.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about monitoring at an active caldera.
* Geologists measured ground tilt with instruments installed on the caldera rim.
* The same stations also recorded rainfall.
* Rain soaking into cracked rock can flex the shallow ground and produce a tilt signal.
* The rim instruments stand 300 meters above the mapped fissure system.

The student wants to explain why geologists recorded rainfall at stations whose purpose was measuring tilt. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Geologists measured ground tilt with instruments installed on the caldera rim, which stands 300 meters above the mapped fissure system. | Rainfall was recorded at the same stations that measured tilt, and those instruments were mounted on the rim of an active caldera. | Since rain soaking into cracked rock can flex the shallow ground and generate a tilt signal, recording rainfall let geologists separate the tilt readings caused by falling water from the readings that came from somewhere else. | Rain soaking into cracked rock can flex the shallow ground, and the fissure system lies about 300 meters below the rim instruments.
explanation: Explaining the point of a measurement step requires the mechanism that makes the step useful, here rain-generated tilt, and the task the recording performs, separating rain-driven readings from others. The third option states both. The first answers where the instruments sit rather than why rainfall was logged, the second reports only that the two instruments shared a station, and the fourth gives the mechanism but then appends the depth of the fissure system, an irrelevant figure that leaves the purpose of the rainfall record unstated.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about biogas output at two farm digesters.
* Digester A produced 1,240 cubic meters of biogas each month from cattle manure.
* Digester B produced 780 cubic meters each month from a mixture of manure and crop residue.
* Digester B ran at a temperature 6 degrees lower than Digester A.
* The two digesters were brought into service in the same year.

The student wants to set the two digesters' monthly output alongside their operating temperatures. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Digester A produced 1,240 cubic meters of biogas per month against Digester B's 780, and Digester B operated at a temperature 6 degrees lower than Digester A. | Digester A produced 1,240 cubic meters of biogas per month from cattle manure, and the two digesters were brought into service in the same year. | The two digesters were brought into service in the same year, and Digester B used a mixture of manure and crop residue. | Digester B produced 780 cubic meters of biogas per month and ran 6 degrees cooler than Digester A, whose feedstock was cattle manure.
explanation: The goal names two variables, output and temperature, so the effective answer reports both for the pair of digesters. The first option gives each monthly figure and the 6-degree difference. The second supplies only one output and adds the commissioning year, the third mentions no output or temperature at all, and the fourth gives Digester B's two figures but reports nothing about Digester A's output, so the quantities are never actually placed side by side.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about competing accounts of canal profitability in the 1840s.
* Canal companies reported an average return on capital of 9 percent in 1843.
* An older study attributed that return to traffic that railways had not yet absorbed.
* A 2019 study reexamined the ledgers of 40 companies and found the returns concentrated among companies holding short-haul bulk contracts.
* The 2019 study also showed that the older study had left six companies out of its sample.

The student wants to emphasize how the 2019 study's explanation of canal returns differs from the older study's explanation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The 2019 study reexamined the ledgers of 40 companies and showed that the older study had left six companies out of its sample. | Canal companies reported an average return on capital of 9 percent in 1843, a return the 2019 study traced to the companies holding short-haul bulk contracts. | The older study attributed canal returns to traffic that railways had not yet absorbed, and canal companies reported an average return of 9 percent in 1843. | Where the older study credited the 9 percent return to traffic railways had not yet absorbed, the 2019 study located the returns in the particular companies that held short-haul bulk contracts.
explanation: Emphasizing a difference between two accounts requires both accounts and an explicit opposition between them, which the last option supplies with a concessive frame. The first describes the newer study's criticisms of the older sample, a point about evidence rather than about the competing explanations. The second gives only the newer account and the third only the older one paired with the headline return, so neither arrangement brings the two explanations into contact.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a claim that ancient DNA was recovered from a bone.
* The laboratory recovered fragments shorter than 40 base pairs from a bone dated to 600,000 years.
* Fragments of similar length were recovered from sterile sediment sampled beside the excavation.
* The recovered sequences matched no living species at more than 70 percent identity.
* The bone's age was estimated from the sediment layer that enclosed it.

The student wants to point out a reason for caution about the claim that the recovered fragments came from the ancient bone. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The laboratory recovered fragments shorter than 40 base pairs, and those sequences matched no living species at more than 70 percent identity. | Because fragments of similar length turned up in sterile sediment sampled beside the excavation, the recovered material may derive from the surrounding deposit rather than from the bone itself. | The bone, dated to 600,000 years, yielded fragments shorter than 40 base pairs. | The sequences matched no living species at more than 70 percent identity, and sterile sediment was sampled beside the excavation.
explanation: A reason for caution has to connect an observation to a specific doubt about the claim. The second option does this, since identical fragments in sterile sediment suggest the bone's material is not the only possible source. The first and third options simply describe what was recovered and the age assigned to the bone, which raises no doubt, and the fourth juxtaposes the weak species match with the existence of sediment samples without stating the implication that makes the sediment evidence troubling.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about playback speeds on early phonograph cylinders.
* Cylinders cut at one plant in 1903 survive at recorded speeds from 78 to 92 revolutions per minute.
* A musicologist replayed twenty of those cylinders on a turntable fixed at 80 revolutions per minute.
* The replayed performances sounded 9 percent faster than the written tempos for the same pieces.
* Cutting motors at this plant were turned by hand and regulated by ear rather than by a governor.

The student wants to account for the tempo discrepancy the musicologist heard. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Because the plant's cutting motors were regulated by ear rather than by a governor, cylinders were cut as fast as 92 revolutions per minute, so replaying them at a fixed 80 revolutions per minute made the performances sound faster than the written tempos. | Cylinders from the plant were cut at speeds ranging from 78 to 92 revolutions per minute, and the musicologist chose twenty of them for replay. | The replayed performances sounded 9 percent faster than the written tempos, and the musicologist obtained that result on a turntable fixed at 80 revolutions per minute. | The musicologist replayed twenty cylinders on a turntable fixed at 80 revolutions per minute, and all of those cylinders date from 1903.
explanation: To account for a surprising measurement, the answer must reach past the setup to the reason the setup produced that outcome, here the unregulated hand-cranked cutting that yielded speeds well above 80. The first option traces that chain. The second gives the observed range and the sample size, the third restates the discrepancy and the playback arrangement, and the fourth adds the cylinders' date, and all three leave the variation in cutting speed, the actual explanation, unmentioned or treated as though the fixed turntable alone produced it.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about corrosion on the glass of a cathedral window.
* Pitting was heavier on the faces of the panes that faced the building's interior than on the faces exposed outside.
* Interior air carried sulfur compounds given off by candles burned during services.
* Rain rinsed the exterior surfaces about 90 times a year.
* All the panes were cast in the same century at a single glasshouse.

The student wants to explain why corrosion concentrated on the interior faces of the panes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: All the panes were cast in the same century at a single glasshouse, so differences in pitting cannot be blamed on differences in casting date or workshop. | Interior air carried sulfur compounds given off by candles, and the panes were cast at a single glasshouse. | Sulfur compounds from candles reached the interior faces, while rain rinsed those exterior faces about 90 times a year, so the attacking agents accumulated inside and were washed away outside. | Rain rinsed the exterior surfaces about 90 times a year, and pitting appeared on the panes of the window.
explanation: The explanation needs both halves of the asymmetry, an agent acting inside and a process relieving the outside, joined to the pattern observed. The third option provides all of that. The first explains what can be ruled out rather than what caused the pitting, the second pairs the interior agent with the irrelevant provenance of the glass, and the fourth notes the rinsing and the presence of pitting without linking either to the interior faces the goal asks about.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about the adoption of milk pasteurization in one country.
* Municipal health officers recommended routine heating of milk in 1899.
* The first city-wide pasteurization bylaw took effect in 1908.
* Infant deaths from digestive disease in that city fell 24 percent between 1908 and 1914.
* A national heating standard was not adopted until 1922.

The student wants to trace the steps from the first official recommendation to the national standard. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The first city-wide pasteurization bylaw took effect in 1908, and infant deaths from digestive disease in the city fell 24 percent between 1908 and 1914. | A national heating standard was adopted in 1922, after infant deaths from digestive disease had fallen 24 percent between 1908 and 1914. | Municipal health officers recommended routine heating of milk in 1899, and the national heating standard was eventually adopted in 1922. | Health officers recommended routine heating in 1899, the first city-wide bylaw then took effect in 1908, and the national standard followed in 1922.
explanation: Tracing a sequence requires every stage in order, and the fourth option places the 1899 recommendation, the 1908 bylaw and the 1922 national standard in that order with explicit connectives. The first stops at the bylaw and turns to a health outcome, the second covers only the last stage and the same mortality figure, and the third gives the two endpoints while omitting the bylaw in between, which leaves the middle of the sequence missing.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a field estimate of a snail population.
* Researchers marked 320 snails with paint and released them.
* Two weeks later they collected 280 snails, 56 of which bore marks.
* The share of marked animals in the second collection was used to estimate the size of the whole population.
* Marked snails were no more likely than unmarked snails to be collected again.

The student wants to describe the procedure the researchers followed in estimating the snail population. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Two weeks after the marking, 280 snails were collected and 56 of them bore marks. | Researchers marked and released 320 snails, collected 280 snails two weeks later, and used the share of marked animals among that second collection to estimate the population. | Marked snails were no more likely than unmarked snails to be collected again, a condition that supports the reliability of the estimate. | The researchers marked and released 320 snails, and 56 of the snails in the second collection bore marks.
explanation: Describing a procedure means giving its steps in order and saying what the steps were for, which the second option does from marking through the calculation. The first reports the second collection alone, leaving out the release that made the ratio meaningful, the third states an assumption about snail behavior that validates the method rather than describing it, and the fourth lists the two counts but never says that the marked share produced the population estimate.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about the treatment of a sixteenth-century wooden altarpiece.
* Conservators removed a varnish layer that had yellowed.
* Analysis showed the original pigment layer beneath the varnish was only 30 micrometers thick.
* Of twelve tests on a sample panel, solvent gels lifted original pigment along with varnish in two.
* The conservators left the outermost 8 micrometers of later overpaint in place.

The student wants to give the conservators' reason for retaining part of the later overpaint. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Since the original pigment layer measured only 30 micrometers and solvent gels lifted pigment along with varnish in two of twelve tests, the conservators kept the outermost 8 micrometers of overpaint rather than risk reaching the original surface. | Analysis showed that the original pigment layer was only 30 micrometers thick, and the yellowed varnish above it was removed. | Solvent gels lifted original pigment in two of twelve tests, and the conservators removed the yellowed varnish layer from the altarpiece. | The conservators left the outermost 8 micrometers of later overpaint in place on an altarpiece made in the sixteenth century.
explanation: A reason has to connect the decision to the evidence that motivated it, and the first option does so by treating the thin pigment layer and the pigment loss in testing as grounds for stopping short. The second and third options report the analysis and the test results but end with the cleaning that was carried out, which is a different action from the one the goal asks about, and the fourth restates the decision along with the object's date, supplying no justification at all.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a survey searching for transiting planets.
* The survey monitored 14,000 stars for repeating dips in brightness.
* A survey instrument recorded one dip each time a star dimmed, but only an object crossing the star's disk produces dips that repeat.
* Three matching dips were required before a candidate was announced.
* The survey announced 46 candidates across four observing seasons.

The student wants to explain the purpose of requiring three matching dips before a candidate was announced. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: The survey monitored 14,000 stars and announced 46 candidates across four observing seasons. | Because a single recorded dip can occur without any object crossing a star's disk, while only such a crossing produces dips that repeat, three matching dips made an announcement less likely to rest on an isolated dimming. | The instrument recorded a dip each time a star dimmed, and the survey monitored 14,000 stars for such events. | Only an object crossing a star's disk produces repeating dips, and the survey announced 46 candidates over four seasons.
explanation: Explaining the purpose of a rule requires the rationale the rule serves, here the difference between a one-off dimming and the repeating dimming that only a true crossing produces, which the second option spells out. The first gives the survey's scale and its tally of candidates, describing the project rather than the rule. The third reports what the instrument recorded without saying why three matches were demanded. The fourth states the principle about crossings correctly but appends the candidate count, so it never connects the rule to the error it guards against.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about boardings on two city bus routes.
* Route 12 recorded 5,100 weekday boardings before its service frequency was doubled.
* After the frequency increase, Route 12 recorded 8,300 weekday boardings.
* Route 44, whose frequency was left unchanged, recorded 4,700 weekday boardings over the same later period.
* Both counts were taken during the same spring month.

The student wants to compare how Route 12's boardings changed with the boardings recorded on Route 44. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Route 12 recorded 8,300 weekday boardings after its frequency was doubled, and both counts were taken during the same spring month. | Route 44 recorded 4,700 weekday boardings, and its frequency was left unchanged during the period. | Both counts were taken during the same spring month, and Route 44's frequency was not altered. | Route 12 rose from 5,100 to 8,300 weekday boardings after its frequency doubled, while Route 44, unchanged in frequency, recorded 4,700 boardings in the same later period.
explanation: The comparison needs Route 12's two figures and Route 44's figure arranged so the reader can see how the routes differ. The last option does exactly that. The first gives only one post-change figure and adds the month the counts were taken, the second reports a single route's numbers, and the third contains no figures at all, mentioning only timing and frequency, so none of them performs the comparison.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about an ice core reconstruction of past snowfall and temperature.
* The core was drilled at a single summit site where snow accumulates at 9 centimeters a year.
* Isotopic temperatures from the core match the region's modelled temperatures after 1950 but depart from them before 1850.
* Volcanic sulfate layers supply the only absolute date markers in the core before 1850.
* No second core from the same ice field was available for comparison.

The student wants to identify what limits confidence in the temperature readings the core provides for the period before 1850. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Isotopic temperatures from the core match the region's modelled temperatures after 1950 but depart from them before 1850. | Because volcanic sulfate layers are the only absolute date markers before 1850 and the reconstruction rests on one summit core with no nearby core for comparison, the pre-1850 departures may reflect uncertainty in dating the layers rather than actual temperature change. | The core was drilled at a summit site where snow accumulates at 9 centimeters a year. | No second core from the same ice field was available, and the core's isotopic temperatures agree with modelled temperatures after 1950.
explanation: Identifying a limit on confidence requires naming a weakness and saying what it calls into question, and the second option links the sparse date markers and single-site record to the status of the pre-1850 readings. The first reports the pattern the reconstruction shows without questioning it, the third gives an accumulation rate that is never tied to any doubt, and the fourth mentions the missing comparison core but pairs it with the post-1950 agreement, a period the goal does not concern.

question:
A student is reviewing notes about a lake's signal crayfish population.
* Crayfish catches fell 62 percent in the three years after a native otter population returned to the lake.
* Otters had been absent from the lake for 40 years before that return.
* Managers had culled crayfish for the five years preceding the return, with no measurable decline.
* In this region otters feed largely on crayfish during winters when fish are scarce.

The student wants to explain why crayfish catches fell only after otters returned rather than during the earlier culling. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish that goal?
options: Regional otters feed largely on crayfish in winters when fish are scarce, and catches at the lake, from which otters had been absent for 40 years, fell 62 percent in the three years after the otters came back. | Managers had culled crayfish at the lake for five years before the otters returned, and that program produced no measurable decline. | Crayfish catches at the lake fell 62 percent, and otters had been absent from the lake for 40 years beforehand. | Otters in the region feed largely on crayfish when fish are scarce in winter, and culling had run at the lake for the five years before the otters returned.
explanation: The explanation needs the mechanism that distinguishes the two periods, namely that returning otters eat crayfish when winter fish run short, together with the drop that followed their arrival. The first option joins those. The second describes the unsuccessful culling, which is the contrast the goal starts from rather than its explanation, the third states the decline and the length of the otters' absence without connecting them, and the fourth supplies the diet fact but pairs it with the timing of the culling and omits the decline itself.

question:
Barcelona's superblock program converts a grid of nine blocks into one unit in which cars may drive only slowly, while the interior streets are handed back to walking, cycling, benches, and play. Evaluations of the first pilot in the Poblenou district recorded less traffic and lower nitrogen dioxide on the reclaimed streets, though some surrounding avenues absorbed the vehicles that were pushed out. City planners argue that the program's significance therefore lies less in the modest change in emissions at any single street than in its demonstration that a municipality can redefine the purpose of a street from moving traffic through a neighborhood to hosting life within it.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The program matters chiefly because it changes what city streets are considered to be for, even though the measured environmental effects on individual streets are limited. | Traffic in Barcelona has been permanently reduced, and the program has eliminated nitrogen dioxide in the neighborhoods it covers. | Traffic displaced onto surrounding avenues cancels whatever environmental benefit a superblock could otherwise produce. | Cycling and street furniture improve neighborhood health more than low-speed vehicle access does.
explanation: For a main-idea question, discard choices that track one sentence instead of the argument. The text concedes that per-street emission changes are modest and then says the real significance is the redefinition of a street's purpose, which is exactly what A states. B is too strong on two counts (permanent reduction, elimination of nitrogen dioxide), C takes the concession about displaced traffic and promotes it into the conclusion the text explicitly rejects, and D turns supporting examples into a comparison the passage never draws.

question:
Popular accounts describe the fungal threads joining the roots of neighbouring plants as a forest internet in which trees generously feed one another. Mycologists point out that the same connections can move defensive compounds between species, that some fungi take more carbon from the partnership than they return, and that isotope-labeling experiments usually find the carbon crossing between plants small next to what one tree fixes in a season. Seedlings of some orchids take all their carbon from the fungus and give nothing back. The evidence supports a narrower claim: the connections are physically real, but what they do depends on which organisms are joined.

Which choice best expresses the central idea of the text?
options: Mycorrhizal fungi are best understood as parasites that reduce the growth of the plants whose roots they colonize. | Popular descriptions have exaggerated cooperation because carbon transfer through fungal threads proves to be negligible in every forest studied. | The belowground connections between plant roots and fungi are genuine, but their ecological effect depends on the species and circumstances involved. | Orchid seedlings show that fungal networks are built to distribute nutrients to whichever plant needs them most.
explanation: This item asks for the claim the whole passage is built to support. The text rejects an exaggerated picture of altruism and then lists cases in which the same network helps, harms, or does nothing, so the balanced conclusion in C is what all the details converge on. A keeps only one of the listed cases and reverses the passage's verdict that the connections are real and consequential; B contains a fair criticism but adds the absolute 'every forest studied,' which the text's hedged word 'usually' does not license; D elevates a single example and, worse, credits the network with a purpose it is not shown to have.

question:
Linguists who study grammaticalization note that an expression with a literal meaning can, over generations of use, acquire a purely grammatical one: English 'be going to' once described physical travel toward a place and now routinely marks future time, and in casual speech the sequence has begun to fuse into 'gonna.' Such shifts are piecemeal, spreading through contexts and speech communities at different rates, so a single variety may carry the older literal use, the newer grammatical use, and the reduced fused form all at once. Changes of this kind are not signs of a language decaying but evidence that grammar is continually rebuilt out of ordinary vocabulary.

Which choice best states the text's central argument?
options: The spread of 'gonna' shows that English's way of marking future time is deteriorating and will eventually replace the older construction. | Grammatical forms can grow out of ordinary words gradually and unevenly, leaving older and newer uses coexisting within one variety. | Expressions in English change their meaning only when they are used to describe physical movement from one place to another. | Speakers of a given community are obliged to choose between a construction's literal sense and its grammatical sense.
explanation: A central-idea answer must cover the mechanism, the pace, and the author's evaluative point, and B does: lexical sources, piecemeal diffusion, coexistence, with the text's rejection of decay left implicit rather than contradicted. A is the distractor the passage is written against, since the final sentence calls this rebuilding rather than decay; C converts one instructive example into an exceptionless 'only'; D asserts a compulsory choice that the described coexistence of three simultaneous forms actually refutes.

question:
Natural-resin varnishes applied over oil paint yellow as they age, so a canvas that left an artist's workshop bright can look uniformly brown a century later. Stripping the varnish can recover the painter's original contrasts, but aggressive cleaning also risks thinning delicate glazes and erasing earlier retouching that has itself become part of the object's history. Arguments over high-profile mid-twentieth-century cleans in London galleries pushed the profession toward recording every layer with microscopy and solvent tests before touching it, and toward leaving aged varnish where its removal cannot be justified. Conservation now treats a painting as a stack of historical events rather than a single moment of making.

Which choice most accurately summarizes the main point of the text?
options: Aged varnish distorts a painting so severely that removing it is required before the artist's own work can be seen at all. | The celebrated mid-twentieth-century cleans in London destroyed irreplaceable glazes and are now judged to have been professional failures. | Retouching added by later restorers deserves to be preserved in preference to whatever glazes the artist originally laid down. | Cleaning has become more cautious because conservators came to value a picture's whole layered history rather than only its appearance at the moment it was painted.
explanation: A summary answer must carry the reorientation the passage builds to, and D carries both halves of it: caution about cleaning, explained by a new regard for the picture's layered history. A contradicts that conclusion, since the text ends by defending leaving aged varnish where removal cannot be justified; B hands down a verdict of destruction and professional failure that the passage only ever implies as a disputed memory; C ranks later retouching above the artist's own glazes, a preference the text refuses to state.

question:
Grain yields in the US Midwest have risen for decades, yet the nitrogen leaving tiled farm fields with spring meltwater has not fallen at a comparable pace, because much cropland stands bare from the autumn harvest until the following planting. Winter rye sown in that interval takes up surplus nitrogen and holds soil in place, and field trials report clear reductions in nitrate loss beneath rye. But rye also withdraws water from the spring profile, and in dry years that withdrawal can offset the yield of the cash crop that follows it. The practice therefore functions less as a finished solution than as a trade-off managed season by season.

Which choice states the central idea of the text most accurately?
options: Rye cover crops reliably reduce nitrogen loss, but their effect on the crop that follows depends on spring moisture, so the net benefit varies from season to season. | Rye cover crops have failed to reduce nitrogen loss from Midwestern fields because tile drainage moves water too quickly for roots to intercept it. | Nitrogen loss has persisted mainly because farmers plant rye later in the autumn than research recommends. | Rye's consumption of soil water disqualifies it for use on any field in the Midwest.
explanation: For main-idea items, look for the choice that holds both halves of the text: the documented benefit and the documented cost. A keeps the trial evidence intact and keeps the moisture-dependent caveat, matching the closing 'trade-off' sentence. B contradicts the trials the text cites; C invents a cause (late planting) that the passage never mentions, replacing the stated reason of bare fallow; D generalizes a conditional problem into an absolute ban.

question:
Before equal temperament became standard on Western keyboards, tunings distributed the unavoidable mismatch between pure fifths and pure octaves unevenly, so some keys sounded smooth and others sounded strained. Composers exploited that inequality: writing in a remote key carried an audible penalty and an audible color at the same time. Even temperament spreads the mismatch identically among all twenty-four major and minor keys, making every key comfortably playable and modulation between distant keys seamless, but it also flattens the distinctions earlier tunings had made perceptible. Performers of Baroque repertoire now weigh the convenience of one tuning against a variety of key character that many modern listeners no longer notice.

Which choice best describes the main idea of the text?
options: Baroque composers generally avoided remote keys because unequal tunings made those keys unplayable. | Equal temperament made the individual intervals of keyboard music purer, which is why the character of the music changed when it was adopted. | Making every key equally playable also erased a distinction between keys that earlier composers had treated as an expressive resource. | Performers of Baroque repertoire have largely abandoned equal temperament in order to recover the sound of the period.
explanation: The passage's argument is a trade-off, so the main idea must name both sides, and C does: universal playability gained, distinction between keys lost. A is wrong on the evidence, since the text says composers exploited remote keys rather than finding them unplayable; B is the technical inversion that trips up many students, because equal temperament slightly detunes each fifth instead of purifying it; D overstates the final sentence, which describes performers weighing a choice rather than a consensus to abandon modern tuning.

question:
In the early 1980s few clinicians expected that a homemade sugar-and-salt solution could rescue children dying of diarrhoeal disease, since replacing fluid through a vein seemed the only treatment serious enough. Oral rehydration, shipped as preweighed sachets and stirred into boiled water, corrected most dehydration at a tiny fraction of the cost, and surveys in several countries recorded large declines in diarrhoeal deaths among young children as its use spread. Historians of public health treat the episode as a case in which a technically simple intervention changed outcomes across whole populations precisely because households could administer it without a clinic.

Which choice best states the primary claim the text makes?
options: Clinics stopped using intravenous rehydration once they learned that it could not correct dehydration. | Oral rehydration's success came largely from the fact that households could carry it out themselves, allowing a simple treatment to save lives on a population scale. | The distribution of preweighed sachets was the only factor that turned oral rehydration into standard treatment. | Clinicians who had doubted oral rehydration later showed that it works better than intravenous fluids.
explanation: B repeats the single move the text makes, that simplicity of delivery is what turned an inexpensive treatment into a population-level gain. A contradicts the passage, which never says intravenous treatment was abandoned or ineffective; C substitutes an absolute, 'the only factor,' for the account of household administration and cost the text actually gives; D claims a comparison between oral and intravenous treatment that the passage never performs.

question:
A space telescope watching tens of thousands of stars flags any regular dimming as a candidate planet, yet the same dip in light can come from an eclipsing pair of stars lying in front of a third, or from noise in the detector. Confirming a world therefore requires independent measurements from the ground, chiefly the star's periodic Doppler shift, which yields the mass of whatever tugs on it. Because such follow-up observations are scarce relative to the number of signals flagged, catalogues list far fewer confirmed planets than the surveys propose. The gap reflects the cost of gathering the second kind of evidence, not weakness in the first.

What is the main idea of the text?
options: Most candidate signals reported by transit surveys turn out to be spurious, so the method cannot be relied upon. | Ground-based Doppler measurements cannot establish the mass of small planets, so most candidates remain permanently unresolved. | Adding more telescopes on the ground would remove the need for confirmation of transit signals altogether. | Far fewer exoplanets are listed as confirmed than as candidates because the independent measurements needed to confirm are limited and costly, not because the initial detections are unreliable.
explanation: A main-idea question is answered by the sentence the others exist to set up, and D restates the cause given there, the cost of independent follow-up measurement rather than any fault in transit detection. A is the conclusion the text refuses to draw; B asserts a limit on Doppler mass measurement the passage never states; C proposes that more ground telescopes would make confirmation unnecessary, whereas the text treats ground-based measurement as exactly what converts a candidate into a confirmed world.

question:
Account rolls from English manors and court records show that labourers' money wages roughly doubled in the decades after the demographic collapse of the mid-fourteenth century, while grain prices fell over the same period, so the purchasing power of a day's work rose steeply. Diets improved and timber-framed houses replaced plainer cottages, though no notable advance in farming technique is recorded. Economic historians therefore treat the episode as one in which living standards were set mainly by the ratio of people to available resources: identical methods fed better-off workers once far fewer of them divided the harvest among.
