Which choice most fully captures the central idea of the text?
options: Living standards in England improved because the balance between population and available output shifted, not because methods of production became more efficient. | The population collapse lowered grain prices, which demonstrates that money wages had fallen behind the cost of living. | Manorial records show that fourteenth-century labourers gained an improvement in living standards that persisted unchanged for centuries afterward. | Advances in farming technique in the mid-fourteenth century raised money wages enough to compensate for falling grain prices.
explanation: The passage pairs a documented rise in real purchasing power with an explicit denial of technical progress, and A is the only choice that preserves that pairing. B is a reversal: wages rose while prices fell, so purchasing power increased rather than lagged; C adds the temporal claim 'for centuries afterward,' which the text's narrower dating does not support; D also reverses causation, since the passage attributes the gain to the changed ratio of people to output and states that technique did not advance.

question:
Nineteenth-century editors seeking the original wording of a border ballad treated every difference between sung copies as corruption of a single lost author's text. Scholars of oral tradition answered that singers carrying a narrative in memory re-make it while performing: stanza order shifts, refrains migrate between lines, and episodes stretch to hold an audience, while the story stays recognizable. On this view the variants are not damage accumulated around an authentic core but the very manner in which the ballad exists, since no fixed text was ever there to depart from. Editing a living tradition is therefore a different task from editing a manuscript an author wrote down.

Which choice best conveys the text's main point?
options: Border ballads cannot be edited responsibly, because singers altered the wording beyond any recovery. | For works carried by singing rather than writing, differences among versions are how the work exists, so editors should not search for one uncorrupted original. | Nineteenth-century editors were the first people to commit border ballads to writing. | Singers preserve a ballad's wording while revising its outline, which is why editors looked for a fixed text.
explanation: The main idea here is the theoretical claim that variation is the medium's normal state, and B also keeps the consequence the text draws for editing. A is the defeatist conclusion the passage declines to draw; C is a historical superlative the text never asserts, since collectors had transcribed ballads long before the nineteenth century; D reverses the described pattern, because the passage says wording changes while the outline stays recognizable.

question:
Around Antarctica in winter, seawater freezing into new ice expels most of its salt into the film of brine beneath, leaving water colder, saltier, and denser than anything nearby. That dense water sinks to the seabed and flows northward through the abyssal layers, carrying oxygen it took up from the atmosphere at the surface. Shipboard measurements along transects across the Atlantic show the bottom water becoming gradually warmer and less salty as it moves toward the equator, mixing with the water masses it passes through. Current meters moored in the deep western boundary channel near South Georgia gauge how much of this water is still being formed.

What does the text report happens to Antarctic Bottom Water as it travels northward?
options: Its oxygen content keeps rising the whole distance toward the equator. | It grows denser still as it mixes with the water masses it encounters. | It becomes warmer and less salty through mixing with the water it passes. | Its flow weakens to a stop near South Georgia.
explanation: Detail questions reward matching an answer to the sentence that actually contains it, and C reports what the transect measurements show, warming and freshening through mixing. A invents a continuing trend, since the text says only that the sinking water carries surface oxygen with it; B is the reversal trap, because maximum density is what makes the water sink at the outset, not something mixing adds later; D misreads the instrument sentence, which presents South Georgia as a place where the flow is measured, not where it stops.

question:
Ceramic vessels from early farming settlements in Central Europe were long assumed not to have held milk, partly because the people who made them carried a genetic signature associated with low lactase persistence, the ability to digest the sugar in fresh milk as adults. Lipid analysis of the pots' walls complicates that assumption. In sherds from several Linearbandkeramik sites, researchers identified fatty acids whose carbon isotope ratios corresponded to ruminant milk fat rather than to the fat of muscle tissue or to plant oils. On this evidence the same scholars proposed that milk was processed into cheese and yoghurt, fermentation of which breaks down much of its lactose.

Which choice identifies the evidence the text cites against the assumption drawn from the genetic signature?
options: The potters who made the vessels carried a genetic signature of low lactase persistence. | Fermenting milk into cheese breaks down much of the lactose it contains. | Settlements of this period produced ceramic vessels used for cooking and storage. | Fatty acids preserved in the vessel walls have isotope ratios corresponding to milk fat rather than to carcass or plant fat.
explanation: Supporting-detail questions turn on the function a sentence performs, and D names the only evidence the text offers against the inherited assumption: isotope ratios in the residue that match milk fat. A is the classic true-but-irrelevant choice, since the genetic signature is the assumption under challenge rather than evidence against it; B is the reconciling mechanism proposed after the residues were measured; C is general background about the vessels that says nothing about their contents.

question:
Transit engineers who time buses at the curb find that most of a vehicle's delay is spent on one part of boarding: riders stepping in at the front door, paying the driver, and shuffling toward the rear of the vehicle. Systems where passengers validate fares at the platform before the bus arrives and board through every door hold dwell times close to those of rail platforms, and a route whose dwell time falls can keep to its timetable with fewer buses in service. Planners building a bus corridor in a Latin American city applied that logic by funding raised station platforms and pre-paid ticketing rather than additional vehicles.

Which choice gives the reason the text offers for treating boarding time as the priority in a bus corridor?
options: Shortening the time a bus spends at the curb can let a route keep its timetable with fewer buses in service. | Buses cost less to operate than rail lines with platform boarding. | Passengers who pay the driver board faster than passengers who board through all doors. | Raised platforms eliminate the need for fare validation at the station.
explanation: The question asks for the stated payoff of cutting dwell time, and A supplies the one the text gives: a route can hold its timetable with fewer buses in service. B compares costs of buses and rail, a comparison the passage never makes, since rail platforms appear only as a benchmark for boarding speed; C reverses the account, because paying the driver at the front door is identified as the slow step; D contradicts the plan described, in which raised platforms and pre-paid validation are funded together.

question:
In time-trial events lasting several minutes, athletes who open far faster than their eventual average are often beaten by athletes who hold an even pace, because an early surge draws on a finite energy reserve while speed is still above what the body can sustain. Sports scientists analysing two-thousand-metre rowing have recorded that crews which spread their power evenly across the distance finish ahead of crews which start quickly, and that the fastest crews of all reserve a short burst for the last few hundred metres. They argue that anaerobic capacity behaves like a battery which empties at a rate that climbs sharply once a threshold intensity is exceeded.

Which choice states what the researchers report about crews racing the two-thousand-metre distance?
options: Crews that start at the highest speed usually finish ahead of crews that pace evenly. | Crews that spread their power evenly finished ahead of crews that started quickly, and the quickest crews kept a burst in reserve for the finish. | Crews that saved nothing for the final stretch recorded the fastest times. | Even pacing produces better times in rowing than in any other time-trial discipline.
explanation: Only B carries both findings the text attributes to the rowing analysis: the superiority of even distribution and the kept burst at the end, and detail questions penalize partial or inverted recall. A is the reversal; C contradicts the reported preference for a final sprint; D generalizes beyond the data by comparing sports that the passage never compares.

question:
Using a head-turn preference procedure, researchers found that six-month-olds who hear only English turned significantly longer toward a speaker who switched from a retroflex to a dental stop, a contrast English does not use to distinguish words. When the same children were tested again between ten and twelve months, they no longer discriminated the switch, whereas infants acquiring Hindi, a language in which that contrast is distinctive, still did. The result is standardly read as perceptual narrowing, a recalibration of attention toward the sound system a child is actually learning, rather than as a general decline in sensitivity to speech sounds.

Which choice describes the difference the text draws between Hindi-learning and English-learning infants at the retest?
options: Only the Hindi-learning infants had been exposed to the contrasting sounds during the study. | The English-learning infants' general sensitivity to speech sounds had declined while the Hindi-learning infants' had not. | The Hindi-learning infants still discriminated the retroflex-dental contrast, whereas the English-learning infants no longer did. | The Hindi-learning infants had failed the six-month test while the English-learning infants had passed it.
explanation: C states the measured difference at retesting: infants acquiring a language that uses the contrast still discriminate it, while the English-learning infants no longer do. A invents an exposure asymmetry the design does not describe; B names precisely the explanation the last sentence rules out, since the text insists the change is not a general decline in sensitivity; D misassigns the six-month result, which was obtained for the English-learning group and never presented as a comparison.

question:
Great tits in temperate woodland time their laying so that the nestlings' peak hunger coincides with the peak abundance of caterpillars, which itself follows the opening of oak buds. Warmer springs advance budbreak and the insect peak, but at a long-term study site in the Netherlands tit laying dates have shifted less than the caterpillars have, so more broods now hatch after the food peak has passed. Rather than counting larvae, researchers index caterpillar abundance by scoring droppings collected on sheets hung beneath the nestboxes, because the larvae are dispersed through the canopy and are easily missed by an observer looking up into it.

What does the text give as a reason for scoring droppings instead of counting larvae directly?
options: Scoring droppings establishes the date of budbreak, which counting larvae cannot. | Scoring droppings showed that laying dates have not kept pace with the caterpillar peak. | Scoring droppings demonstrates that nestlings feed on caterpillars rather than on other insects. | Larvae spread through the canopy are hard to observe, so droppings collected below register insects that visual surveys miss.
explanation: The text justifies the method on a single ground, detection, and D states it: dispersed larvae are easy to miss by eye, whereas droppings fall predictably onto sheets below. A attributes to frass something measured on the trees; B reports a real finding of the study that comes from nest records and warming data, a true detail fastened to the wrong instrument; C asserts a dietary comparison the passage never makes.

question:
Prices across much of Western Europe rose roughly sixfold over the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, an increase long explained by the arrival of silver mined at Potosi and in New Spain. Annual series of wheat prices from Castilian markets, however, indicate that the climb was under way before large fleets were carrying bullion north, while parish and census reconstructions show substantially more people living on harvests of comparable size through the same decades. Scholars now tend to divide the credit between new silver and population growth, observing that the increase in money wages lagged prices and that many labouring households were purchasing less, not more, as the century advanced.

Which choice names the observation about Castilian markets that the text presents as a difficulty for a purely silver-based account?
options: Prices rose roughly sixfold over the two centuries in question. | Series show the rise in wheat prices beginning before substantial bullion reached Europe. | Silver mined at Potosi was frequently debased before it was shipped. | Money wages failed to keep pace with rising prices.
explanation: The difficulty the text raises is one of sequence, and B is the observation that creates it: in Castile prices appear to turn upward before the bullion fleets are carrying silver in quantity, whereas a purely monetary cause should lag the inflow. A names the phenomenon the silver story was designed to explain, not evidence against it; C introduces debasement, which the passage never mentions; D reports a further consequence of rising prices that would follow from any cause of them.

question:
Before 1925, records were cut mechanically: sound gathered in a horn moved a stylus that scribed the groove, and a forte passage for brass could drive that stylus out of the wall of the groove, so bands played softly, close to the mouth of the horn, largely in unison. With the arrival of the microphone and electrical recording, a double bass, a breathy vocal, and a sustained note inside a bar all became capturable, and arrangers began to distribute a melody across sections instead of doubling it. Jazz historians treat the big-band arrangement of the 1930s as partly a consequence of this technical change rather than as a purely aesthetic turn.

Which choice states the effect of electrical recording on arrangements that the text describes?
options: It allowed quiet, low-pitched, and sustained parts to be captured, so arrangers could spread a melody across sections rather than doubling it. | It allowed brass players to perform far louder than they had in front of an acoustic horn. | It caused collective improvisation to displace written arrangement in the 1930s. | It made the recording horn obsolete as a source of income for arrangers.
explanation: A carries the single consequence the text attributes to the microphone: sounds too quiet or too low for a horn could now be captured, so a melody could be distributed across sections rather than doubled. B infers the opposite licence, greater loudness, when the passage stresses the newly recordable softness; C reverses the direction of the change, since electrical recording is credited with the rise of arranged writing, not with its replacement by looser collective playing; D is close enough in vocabulary to tempt a skimming reader but states a conclusion about arrangers' income that appears nowhere.

question:
European robins migrating by night orient with an inclination compass that depends on the Earth's magnetic field, and birds in the laboratory exposed to weak radio-frequency noise in the medium-wave band lose their orientation. One hypothesis holds that such noise interferes with the light-dependent chemical reaction in the retina believed to supply the magnetic sense, since fields of that strength are far too weak to warm tissue. Researchers released migrating robins in wooden shelters beside an active broadcast transmitter, and released a second group in identical shelters enclosed in a metal mesh that lets the magnetic field through but blocks radio waves.

Which choice describes a finding that, if true, would most support the hypothesis about migrating robins stated in the text?
options: Birds in the unscreened shelters oriented inconsistently while birds in the mesh-screened shelters oriented consistently. | Birds in both kinds of shelter oriented equally well. | The screened shelters were measurably several degrees warmer than the unscreened ones. | Birds released near the transmitter flew longer distances during the night.
explanation: Evaluating evidence for a hypothesis means testing its distinguishing prediction, and here the hypothesis requires that removing radio waves alone restores orientation while the geomagnetic field stays the same, which is precisely what A reports. B is the result that would falsify the hypothesis; C supplies a confound, since a temperature difference inside the screened shelters would offer a non-magnetic explanation of any effect; D reports a variable the study does not measure and that bears on stamina rather than on compass calibration.

question:
Teenagers who use screens late at night fall asleep later and sleep shorter, and a familiar explanation is that short-wavelength light from displays suppresses the evening rise in melatonin and so shifts the timing of sleep. A sleep clinic measured the onset of melatonin secretion in adolescents after an hour of evening device use and found it delayed. A rival explanation blames not the light but the material, since stimulating content raises cognitive arousal and a teenager reading the same text on paper might stay up just as late. The two explanations make different predictions about what happens when identical content is delivered without short-wavelength light.

Which choice describes a finding that, if true, would most call into question the light-based explanation?
options: Fitting the same display with a short-wavelength filter left reported alertness unchanged. | The delay in melatonin onset after an hour of reading identical text on paper matched the delay measured after the unfiltered screen. | Pupils constricted more under the unfiltered screen than under the filtered one. | Teenagers who used devices late reported more daytime sleepiness than those who did not.
explanation: To undercut a light-based account, an observation must remove light as the variable while holding content constant, and B delivers exactly that by producing the same hormonal shift through a route containing no screen light at all. A is a finding about subjective alertness, the rival account's variable rather than the melatonin measure, so it does not bear on the light claim; C describes the first step of the light mechanism and so supports it; D merely restates the correlation the hypothesis is meant to explain.

question:
Reservoirs flooded over boreal soils in Canada tend to accumulate methylmercury in their fish, and sulphate-reducing bacteria living in oxygen-poor sediment carry out the methylation. Researchers hypothesise that the recent rise in mercury measured in one reservoir reflects methylation stimulated by sulphate arriving from upstream mine effluent rather than additional mercury delivered from the atmosphere. Their reasoning is that bacterial methylation should scale with the sulphate available to the bacteria, whereas mercury settling from air would be spread fairly evenly across an entire lake district and should not concentrate toward an inflow.

Which choice describes a finding that, if true, would most support the researchers' hypothesis about the reservoir?
options: Fish taken throughout the reservoir showed mercury levels indistinguishable from those in distant lakes downwind of industrial regions. | Sulphate-reducing bacteria were recovered from sediment cores at every lake sampled, including lakes whose fish contained little mercury. | Mercury in fish was far higher in the arm nearest the mine outfall than at the outlet end of the same reservoir, while lakes elsewhere in the district showed no such gradient. | The effluent also carries fine suspended sediment that smothers spawning grounds for some distance downstream.
explanation: The hypothesis predicts a spatial signature, since effluent-fed methylation should peak near the source while airborne mercury should be flat across a district, and C reports that gradient inside the reservoir alongside its absence elsewhere. A supports the rival atmospheric explanation; B shows the bacteria are ubiquitous and therefore cannot explain why only this reservoir's fish accumulate mercury, so it weakens rather than supports the claim; D concerns a different environmental harm that bears nothing on the origin of the methylmercury.

question:
Stellar models give the young Sun roughly seventy percent of its present brightness four billion years ago, yet the planet's oldest surviving rocks indicate liquid water at the surface, and oxygen isotope ratios in the earliest dated minerals point to seawater at temperatures close to modern ones. That mismatch is the faint young Sun problem. One proposed solution is a much thicker blanket of greenhouse gases, mainly carbon dioxide and methane, in the early atmosphere. If forcing from gases compensated for the dimmer Sun, the geological record of that interval should show persistent liquid water and no planetwide glaciation.

Which choice describes a finding that, if true, would most support the proposed solution to the faint young Sun problem?
options: Isotopes from rocks of that interval worldwide record ocean temperatures consistently below the freezing point of fresh water. | Zircon grains from western Australia dated to the dimmest interval indicate liquid seawater at near-modern temperatures, and no glacial deposits of that age have been identified anywhere. | Climate simulations with today's greenhouse gas concentrations reproduce today's global mean surface temperature. | The same minerals that record seawater also record a heavy bombardment of meteorites ending around that time.
explanation: The solution is credited only if the record shows unfrozen water during the dimmest period and lacks a global ice sheet, which is the conjunction B provides. A contradicts both halves of the prediction; C is a model validation at the wrong date and so bears nothing on the Archean atmosphere; D is background about impacts, which neither confirms nor challenges greenhouse warming.

question:
Wheat contains fructans, short-chain carbohydrates that some people absorb poorly, and reports of feeling better eating sourdough than ordinary bread are frequently credited to the lactic acid bacteria in the starter, which can break these compounds down during fermentation. A food-science team hypothesised instead that the amount of fructan remaining in a loaf depends on the length and warmth of the fermentation, not on the presence of live bacteria as such. They analysed residual fructan in loaves made from a traditional starter under a short cool schedule and a long warm one.

Which choice describes a result that, if true, would most weaken the food scientists' hypothesis?
options: Loaves made with a starter heat-treated to kill its bacteria retained similar amounts of fructan under both the short cool and the long warm schedules. | Longer, warmer fermentation lowered residual fructan in every loaf the team analysed. | Volunteers who ate the sourdough loaves reported less bloating than those who ate ordinary bread. | The bacterial species present in starters differed markedly from one bakery's sourdough to another's.
explanation: The hypothesis is that schedule alone drives fructan loss, so A is decisive: if the long warm schedule makes no difference once the bacteria are dead, then the schedule had been working through them. B is the result the hypothesis predicts and so strengthens it; C reports the consumer experience that motivated the study without touching the mechanism; D describes variation between starters without connecting it to residual fructan.

question:
Students who study a word list once and then attempt to recall it remember more a week later than students who restudy the list the same number of times, even though the first group spends no extra time with the material. One account explains this testing effect through the effort of retrieval, which is said to leave a memory trace that is easier to use later. A rival account attributes the difference to spacing, arguing that taking a test naturally pushes the second encounter with the words further away from the first. The accounts can be separated by giving the restudy group an equal gap before its second pass.

Which choice describes a result that, if obtained, would most support the retrieval-effort account over the spacing account?
options: The tested group and the restudied group recalled equally well when the second encounter with the words followed the first immediately. | Students who took the practice recall test judged their own learning more confidently than those who restudied. | The advantage of testing grew larger for lists of unrelated words than for lists of related ones. | Tested students outremembered restudied students who were given the same total study time and an identical gap before their second pass.
explanation: Two rival explanations are separated only by holding one of them fixed, and D keeps the interval identical in both groups while retrieval still differs, which is what an effect of retrieval effort requires. A is the result favouring the spacing account, since the advantage vanishes as soon as no interval exists; B reports confidence rather than retention, and confidence judgments can move independently of what is remembered; C concerns the relatedness of word lists, a variable neither account singles out, so it does not separate them.

question:
Assigning authorship to undated Elizabethan drama relies partly on function words: researchers count how often a play uses items such as 'and', 'but', 'with', and 'by', on the reasoning that such choices are made beneath conscious attention and differ measurably between writers. A play first printed in 1608 has been assigned to one dramatist on stylistic grounds, although its versification changes abruptly near the middle. Scholars testing that assignment compared the function-word profile of each half of the play, and of the whole, against profiles built from printed works by two dramatists known to have shared a theatrical company.

Which choice describes a finding that, if true, would best support the claim that the 1608 play had two authors?
options: The versification change near the middle of the play coincides with the end of the third act. | Function-word frequencies are stable across the surviving solo works of each of the two dramatists. | The profile of each half matched one of the two dramatists closely, while the profile of the whole play matched neither as well. | The play as printed in 1608 is the only surviving copy of the text.
explanation: Co-authorship predicts discontinuity at exactly the seam the text notices, so finding each half close to a different author and the combined text matching neither is the signature C reports. A describes where the shift falls in the play's structure without connecting it to either candidate author; B states the methodological premise that makes the test usable but says nothing about this play; D concerns the survival of the document rather than the identity of its writers.

question:
Researchers tracking reef fish larvae in a turbid lagoon found that settling larvae attached overwhelmingly to panels whose speakers had replayed a dense chorus of resident fish, and avoided panels whose speakers had stayed silent. Larvae in the lagoon detect light but cannot resolve shapes beyond a few centimetres, and in a flume experiment the same preference appeared after chemical cues carried in the water had been filtered out. The researchers therefore propose that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the acoustic chorus is the only factor that determines where reef fish larvae settle. | reefs hosting dense fish populations are safer places for larvae than quiet reefs are. | sound can help larvae choose a settlement site when they cannot make use of visual or chemical information. | larvae that settle on quiet reefs are unlikely to survive to adulthood.
explanation: This item asks what conclusion the described evidence strictly permits. Only a choice that follows from both observations, the preference for noisy panels and the persistence of that preference once chemical cues were removed, is defensible: C says exactly that. A turns a demonstrated cue into the sole determinant, which the experiment never tested; B imports safety, a variable nobody measured; D predicts adult survival from a settlement choice recorded hours or days earlier.

question:
Forty bilingual children and forty monolingual children repeated unfamiliar words in a language none of them spoke, and the two groups performed almost identically. In a second task the bilingual children named pictures faster in the language they used every day than in the language they used once a week, whereas the monolingual children, who had a single language, showed no comparable gap. The second task suggests that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: quicker retrieval reflects how often a language is used rather than how many languages a speaker knows. | bilingual children name pictures more quickly than monolingual children do. | children cannot retrieve vocabulary from a language used only once a week. | monolingual children would name pictures faster if they studied a second language.
explanation: The skill is spotting which variable the design actually manipulated: within the bilingual group the only difference was frequency of use, and the between-group comparison showed no advantage at all. A tracks that pattern. B is flatly contradicted by the first task, C converts a slowing into a total inability, and D recommends or predicts an outcome no child in the study produced.

question:
Excavations at a site in northern Mexico produced obsidian blades chemically matched to a source about 300 kilometres away. Every matched blade came from a single workshop layer dated to a span of roughly sixty years, while the layers immediately above and below it, formed by the same community, contain only obsidian from a source within 60 kilometres. No trace of permanent residence at the distant source has been found. Because the community evidently occupied the site before and after the workshop layer, the blades suggest that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the community left the site within sixty years after the workshop layer was formed. | obsidian from the nearer source was of lower quality than the imported material. | the community's overall use of obsidian collapsed once the workshop layer was laid down. | the long-distance supply depended on a brief arrangement rather than on a settled, long-standing practice.
explanation: Here the evidence is a pattern confined to one thin layer, so the licensed conclusion is that whatever brought the distant stone was temporally restricted; D states that without inventing a mechanism. A contradicts the stated continuity of occupation, B asserts a quality difference no analyst measured, and C misreads which variable changed, since the community went on using obsidian from the nearer source.

question:
Records from twelve rural clinics show that clinics which opened early and required appointments for chronic-disease follow-ups reported lower no-show rates than clinics that accepted walk-ins throughout the day. The researchers gathered no information on how far patients lived from their clinic, on household income, or on how advanced the patients' conditions were. On the records alone, the researchers can most reasonably claim that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: clinics that require appointments can expect to lower their no-show rates. | the records show a link between scheduling practice and attendance but cannot by themselves show that the practice caused the difference. | patients at walk-in clinics generally live farther from their clinics than patients at appointment clinics do. | no-show rates are lowest where patients are healthiest.
explanation: The tested skill is separating an association from a causal claim when the study measured only one pairing. B is exactly as strong as cross-sectional records can be, and it also flags that unmeasured factors might explain the pattern. A drops the hedge and asserts causation, while C and D name variables the study explicitly did not measure, so neither can be a finding.

question:
A musicologist compared tempo markings in surviving autograph scores of a nineteenth-century composer's orchestral movements with metronome figures the composer wrote for the same movements in a treatise compiled near the end of his life. For thirty-four of the forty-one movements the two figures agree within five beats per minute. For the other seven, all of them early works, the treatise figure is ten to twenty-five beats slower, and the autographs of those seven were never revised. The discrepancy is best explained by the possibility that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the composer's metronome gave unreliable readings whenever a tempo was fast. | an assistant copying the treatise misread several of the composer's figures. | the composer's preferred speeds for the early works shifted late in life, so the unaltered autographs preserve an earlier practice than the treatise does. | tempo markings in autograph scores are of little use to performers today.
explanation: This inference requires two steps: the disagreements are confined to early works, and the treatise is late, so what separates the two records is time, not the notation itself. C links those facts. A and B invent instrument error or scribal error to explain a pattern neatly clustered by date of composition, and D concludes from two documents that autograph markings are generally useless.

question:
Across three season-long field trials, plots amended with biochar held between 8 and 14 percent more soil moisture than unamended plots during dry spells. In years with above-average rainfall the amended plots yielded about the same as the unamended ones, while in the driest year they yielded 11 percent more. The trials indicate that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the yield benefit of biochar appeared mainly when water was limiting, so the amendment may add little in seasons with ample rain. | biochar raises crop yields by 8 to 14 percent. | soil moisture rather than rainfall determines a crop's final yield. | amending plots with biochar lets farmers reduce irrigation by 11 percent.
explanation: The question tests whether you keep a conclusion inside the range of the measured conditions: the yield effect shows up only in the dry year, so A's restriction to water-limited seasons is exactly what the pattern supports. B borrows the moisture figures and relabels them as yield gains, C settles a general causal question the trials never isolated, and D extends a rainfall result to irrigation the trials never manipulated.

question:
After a city deleted the rule requiring new downtown apartments to include parking, developers of eleven buildings provided an average of 0.2 spaces per unit instead of the 0.7 that had been required. Rents in those buildings did not fall, and a survey found that a smaller share of their residents commuted by car than in comparable older buildings. Before the reform, developers built the required spaces and recovered the construction cost through rent. The evidence best supports the conclusion that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: deleting parking requirements reliably lowers rents for new housing. | the fall in driving was caused by the unchanged rents. | most residents of the new buildings no longer own a car. | savings from building less parking did not reach tenants as lower rents, since rents held steady as parking costs dropped.
explanation: The reasoning chain is short: if the old cost had been passed on through rent, a smaller parking cost would have lowered rent, and rent did not fall. D states that. A is contradicted by the flat rents, B invents a causal link between two figures that were never compared as cause and effect, and C inflates a smaller share into a majority owning no car.

question:
In a blinded crossover trial, ten competitive cyclists completed a 40-kilometre time trial 2.1 percent faster on average after taking a caffeine lozenge than after taking a placebo lozenge of identical taste. Laboratory tests run before the trial found no difference between the two conditions in the cyclists' lactate thresholds, a measure commonly used to predict endurance performance. Because the lozenge was taken shortly before each ride, the trial supports the inference that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: caffeine improves performance only over distances as long as 40 kilometres. | the faster rides are unlikely to have been mediated by a change in lactate threshold, which stayed constant while performance improved. | lactate threshold is a poor predictor of endurance performance in cyclists generally. | an improvement of 2.1 percent is too small for athletes to take seriously.
explanation: The hard move is reading a null result narrowly: the same riders performed better on a measure while an unrelated laboratory measure of the same physiology was unchanged, so B follows that the improvement was not routed through that measure. C makes the much stronger claim the null result cannot carry, since threshold may still rank riders against one another. A adds a distance restriction nobody tested, and D replaces a measurement with a value judgement.

question:
Two early printed editions of a seventeenth-century poem differ in fifty-one places. Eleven of the differences correct errors that editors agree were introduced by the printer of edition A. The other forty readings appear in neither edition A nor the single surviving manuscript, and several of them turn irregular lines into regular ones. No annotated copy of edition A in the poet's hand has ever been found. On this evidence alone a scholar can argue that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: edition B must have been set from a second manuscript that has since been lost. | edition A is unreliable and should be disregarded by later editors. | some of the forty additional readings probably reflect an editor's taste for regular metre rather than recovered words of the poet. | the poet revised the poem to regularise its metre after edition A appeared.
explanation: Editorial inference of this kind weighs which agent the described pattern implicates: readings that smooth metre and match no surviving source are the signature of a house style, which is what C claims, and the words 'on this evidence alone' matter. A posits an undocumented manuscript as though the forty readings forced it, D assigns the same smoothing to the poet with no evidence at all, and B discards an entire edition because of the forty disputed variants, including the eleven corrections that editors accept.

question:
Between 1780 and 1820 the number of wills proved each year in one English county roughly tripled, while the county's population grew by only a fifth. Historians have often read the extra wills as proof that more households held property worth leaving. Yet county records show that legal changes in the 1790s sharply reduced the fees a household paid to prove a will, and that the average value of estates entering probate fell throughout the same decades. The records suggest that ____

Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: part of the rise in proved wills may reflect the growing affordability of probate, which drew in modest households rather than signalling larger estates. | households in the county became poorer on average between 1780 and 1820. | the legal changes altered the contents of wills as well as their length. | the lower fees caused testators to write wills that ran to more pages.
explanation: This is the classic move of finding an alternative explanation the numbers make available: a cost reduction plus a falling average estate value loosens the link between will counts and accumulating wealth, and 'may reflect' keeps the claim at the strength the evidence allows. B mistakes the average value of probated estates for the wealth of all households, and C and D assert facts about contents or length that no recorded number speaks to.

question:
A government review lists the share of each of two countries' sea territory under formal protection.

Country X in 2012: 2.1 percent of national waters
Country X in 2022: 8.4 percent of national waters
Country Y in 2012: 6.0 percent of national waters
Country Y in 2022: 6.3 percent of national waters

Which choice most effectively uses the figures to complete the comparison of how quickly the two countries expanded protection between 2012 and 2022?
options: In 2022 Country X protected a larger area of sea than Country Y did. | Country X's protected share rose by 6.3 percentage points while Country Y's rose by only 0.3, so that by 2022 X's share was the higher of the two. | Country Y's protected share fell between 2012 and 2022. | Country X's protected share in 2012 stood at 8.4 percent, well above Country Y's figure.
explanation: The skill is reading two normalised figures as changes rather than as levels: subtracting within each country gives 6.3 points for X against 0.3 for Y, and the endpoint comparison (8.4 against 6.3) is also true, so B captures the actual pattern. A converts shares of territories of unknown size into square kilometres nobody reported. C reverses a rise of 0.3 points into a fall, and D assigns X's 2022 value to the year 2012.

question:
A metropolitan transit authority's performance summary for Light Rail Line 1 gives these figures. The summary is drawn from the authority's own annual reports, which apply a single counting method in both years.

Weekday boardings in 2019: 84,000
Weekday boardings in 2023: 121,000
Average peak-period delay in 2019: 3.4 minutes
Average peak-period delay in 2023: 5.1 minutes

Which choice most effectively uses the summary to support an analyst's claim that ridership on Line 1 grew with no gain in punctuality?
options: Average peak-period delay in 2023 was 5.1 minutes, the highest figure Line 1 has ever recorded. | Line 1 carried 121,000 passengers each weekday in 2023, so the authority must have run more trains. | Delay averaged 3.4 minutes in 2019 and boardings averaged 121,000 in 2023, so the line became both fuller and more punctual. | Weekday boardings rose by 37,000 between 2019 and 2023 while average peak-period delay rose by 1.7 minutes over the same period.
explanation: A claim about two variables moving together needs both changes measured over the same interval, and D supplies them: 121,000 minus 84,000 boardings against 1.7 minutes of additional delay. A reports one endpoint and adds an all-time high the summary does not establish. B infers service frequency, which is not tabulated, from a boarding count. C pairs one figure from each year and so manufactures a punctuality gain that the matched-year figures show as a loss.

question:
An agronomist's trial table records wheat plots grown with slow-release urea and with conventional urea.

Yield, slow-release urea, 2021: 6.8 tonnes per hectare
Yield, slow-release urea, 2022: 7.4 tonnes per hectare
Yield, conventional urea, 2021: 6.5 tonnes per hectare
Yield, conventional urea, 2022: 6.6 tonnes per hectare
Nitrogen lost as gas, slow-release treatment: 9.1 percent of nitrogen applied
Nitrogen lost as gas, conventional treatment: 15.6 percent of nitrogen applied

Which choice most effectively uses the table to complete the statement that the slow-release treatment performed better in both measured respects?
options: Slow-release plots outyielded conventional plots in each year, with the gap widening from 0.3 to 0.8 tonnes per hectare, and they lost a smaller percentage of applied nitrogen as gas. | The slow-release treatment lost 15.6 percent less nitrogen as gas than the conventional treatment lost. | Conventional plots yielded 6.6 tonnes per hectare in 2021, a figure that the slow-release plots exceeded. | Because the slow-release plots lost less nitrogen as gas, less nitrogen in total must have been applied to them.
explanation: The task is to match a two-part claim with two-part evidence, and A does so: yearly yields of 6.8 against 6.5 and 7.4 against 6.6 show a widening gap, while 9.1 percent against 15.6 shows the loss advantage. B hands the conventional treatment's own share to the difference, which is 6.5 percentage points. C reports the 2022 conventional yield but dates it to 2021. D treats a share of what was applied as though it revealed how much was applied, which the table never states.

question:
A regional health board's table records measles outcomes in two districts.

District North, second-dose coverage in 2020: 61 percent
District North, second-dose coverage in 2023: 88 percent
District North, reported measles cases in 2020: 143
District North, reported measles cases in 2023: 19
District South, second-dose coverage in 2020: 79 percent
District South, second-dose coverage in 2023: 84 percent
District South, reported measles cases in 2020: 60
District South, reported measles cases in 2023: 34

Which choice most effectively uses the table to complete the claim that District North improved on both measures by more than District South did?
options: District North had the higher second-dose coverage of the two districts in 2020. | District South's reported cases fell from 60 to 34, a larger reduction than District North achieved. | North's coverage rose by 27 percentage points against South's 5, while North's reported cases fell by 124 and South's by 26. | North reported just 19 cases in 2023 because 12 percent of its population had measles.
explanation: To show improvement on two measures the choice must compute the same interval in both districts and in both series, which C does: 88 minus 61 against 84 minus 79, and 143 minus 19 against 60 minus 34. A reads the wrong year, when South led on coverage. B reverses the case comparison, since 26 fewer cases is far less than 124. D confuses the 12 percent of people lacking a second dose with a share of people infected.

question:
A conservation laboratory exposed two coloured samples to a fixed light source and recorded total colour change on the Delta E scale, where larger numbers mean more visible alteration.

Sample A after 200 hours of exposure: 3.1 units
Sample A after 600 hours of exposure: 6.8 units
Sample B after 200 hours of exposure: 1.4 units
Sample B after 600 hours of exposure: 2.2 units

Which choice most effectively uses the laboratory's records to support the conservator's conclusion that Sample A is the more light-sensitive of the two?
options: Sample A's recorded change of 6.8 units is nearly five times Sample B's change of 1.4 units, which shows that the light source weakened as the trial ran. | Over the additional 400 hours Sample A's recorded change grew by 3.7 units, more than four times the growth of 0.8 units recorded for Sample B. | Sample B changed less than Sample A at both measurements, which shows that Sample B's colour was unchanged during the first 200 hours. | Both samples changed more after 600 hours than after 200 hours, so exposure time had a smaller effect on Sample A than on Sample B.
explanation: Sensitivity is a rate of change per unit of exposure, so the comparison must be made between equal intervals: from 200 to 600 hours A gained 3.7 units and B only 0.8, which is B's arithmetic and its logic. A compares figures taken at unequal exposure times and then adds an unmeasured claim about the lamp. C treats a smaller change as though it were no change, and D reverses the direction of the comparison.

question:
A metropolitan transport plan reports the following figures.

Kilometres of protected bike lane in 2010: 46
Kilometres of protected bike lane in 2024: 178
Bike commuters as a share of the commuter workforce in 2010: 3.0 percent
Bike commuters as a share of the commuter workforce in 2024: 9.6 percent
Commuter workforce in 2010: 210,000
Commuter workforce in 2024: 322,000

Which choice most effectively uses the plan to complete the claim that cycling grew in absolute terms faster than the share figures alone would suggest?
options: Because bike commuters more than tripled as a share of the workforce, the number of bike commuters also tripled. | The length of protected lane grew by 132 percent between 2010 and 2024, while cycling's share grew by 6.6 points. | In 2024 the city had 30,900 more bike commuters than it had had in 2010. | The bike-commuter count rose from about 6,300 to roughly 30,900, nearly a fivefold increase, because the share more than tripled while the workforce itself grew by about half.
explanation: Converting shares into counts requires the third row of data, the changing size of the workforce: 3.0 percent of 210,000 is about 6,300 and 9.6 percent of 322,000 is about 30,900, so growth in the count outruns growth in the share, as D says. A applies the share's multiple to the count and so ignores the growing base, which is the error the question is built to catch. B reports the 132 added kilometres as 132 percent. C states the resulting count as though it were the increase, which is nearer to 24,600.

question:
A strength and conditioning coach recorded two training groups across an eight-week program.

Group 1: 3 sessions per week; 5-kilometre run time before the program: 26 minutes 40 seconds; after eight weeks: 24 minutes 10 seconds
Group 2: 5 sessions per week; 5-kilometre run time before the program: 26 minutes 35 seconds; after eight weeks: 25 minutes 0 seconds

Which choice most effectively uses the coach's records to support the claim that Group 1 improved more while spending less time training?
options: Group 1 removed 2 minutes 30 seconds from its run time over 24 total sessions, whereas Group 2 removed 1 minute 35 seconds over 40 sessions. | Group 2 removed 1 minute 35 seconds, an improvement equal to Group 1's. | Group 1 ended with a time of 24 minutes 10 seconds, which means its run time fell by that amount. | Group 2 trained 5 sessions per week and so completed 40 fewer sessions than Group 1.
explanation: Supporting a two-part claim needs both the time change and the session total: 26 minutes 40 seconds down to 24 minutes 10 seconds is 2 minutes 30 seconds, and three sessions a week for eight weeks is 24, which A pairs against Group 2's smaller gain from more sessions. B equates two unequal improvements, C confuses a final time with the amount of change, and D reverses the session counts, since 40 is more than 24.

question:
A corpus linguist compared two collections of student essays.

1995 collection: 1.2 million words in total; 47,000 tokens of the construction think that per million words
2015 collection: 1.6 million words in total; 31,000 tokens of the same construction per million words

Which choice most effectively uses the comparison to show that the construction's decline is milder in raw counts than in normalised rates?
options: The 2015 collection must contain fewer essays than the 1995 collection contains. | The rate fell by 16,000 tokens per million words, so the total number of tokens of the construction also fell by 16,000. | Tokens per million fell by about a third, from 47,000 to 31,000, while total tokens for the construction went from roughly 56,400 to roughly 49,600, a fall of about an eighth. | The 1995 rate of 47,000 tokens per million words means that nearly one word in twenty-five in that collection was the construction think that.
explanation: The point of a normalised rate is that raw totals also depend on collection size, so multiplying out is required: 47 tokens per thousand times 1.2 million words is about 56,400, and 31 per thousand times 1.6 million is about 49,600, a much gentler decline than the rate's, as C states. B equates the two declines, which is the mistake the item punishes. A reads a larger word count as more essays, and D divides 47,000 by a million, treating the rate as a share of the collection.

question:
An archival study plotted the apparent brightness of a variable star on six nights spread across a month, using the magnitude scale on which smaller numbers denote brighter objects. The curve runs steadily upward from magnitude 12.4 on the first night to magnitude 13.1 on the fifth, then drops to magnitude 12.6 on the sixth. The same observatory's calibration was unchanged throughout.

Which choice most effectively uses the plotted values to complete the description of the star's behaviour over the month?
options: The star grew steadily brighter from the first night to the fifth and faded on the sixth. | The star dimmed across the first five nights, because rising magnitudes denote fading light, and the lower magnitude on the sixth night marks a partial recovery. | The star was dimmest on the sixth night, when its magnitude stood at 12.6. | Between the fifth and sixth nights the star's magnitude changed by 12.6.
explanation: Reading this graph depends on knowing that the magnitude scale runs opposite to brightness, so climbing numbers mean a dimming star and the final drop means a brightening; B holds both directions right. A applies an intuitive but inverted reading of the scale. C calls the sixth night dimmest when the highest, and therefore dimmest, value was recorded on the fifth. D reports a plotted value as though it were the interval, which is 0.5 magnitudes.

question:
A streaming-industry brief describes a chart tracking, for each year from 2016 to 2024, the share of tracks on the fifty highest-ranked playlists that were sung in a language other than English. That share rose from 6 percent in 2016 to 19 percent in 2024, and every list in the survey continued to hold exactly fifty tracks. The brief notes that the remaining slots on a list include both English-language songs and purely instrumental pieces.

Which choice most effectively uses the chart to complete the brief's account of what happened to the number of non-English tracks per list?
options: It rose from 6 to 19 tracks per list, since every list holds fifty tracks. | It more than tripled, which shows that English-language songs had been dropped from the lists by 2024. | It stayed roughly constant, because the number of slots on each list never changed. | It rose from three tracks to about nine or ten per list, and although the residual share fell from 94 to 81 percent, that residual need not be English singing, since it also holds instrumental pieces.
explanation: Converting a share of a fixed total is the skill here: 6 percent and 19 percent of fifty slots are three and nine-and-a-half tracks, and D pairs that with the correct caution about the leftover categories named in the brief. A transcribes percentage points into track counts. B treats the residual 81 percent as though it were automatically English singing. C confuses a constant total with constant parts.

question:
A wildlife agency's report describes a line graph of the percentage of monitored songbird nests destroyed by predators in each of three survey years. The rate fell from 22 percent in 2018 to 18 percent in 2021 and 15 percent in 2024, while the number of nests the agency monitored rose from 100 in 2018 to 400 in 2024.

Which choice most effectively uses the graphed trend to complete the report's statement about nest losses?
options: The proportion of monitored nests lost declined, yet the number of predated nests implied by the figures grew from 22 in 2018 to 60 in 2024, because many more nests were under watch. | Fewer nests were destroyed by predators in 2024 than in 2018, because the rate was lower. | The predation rate fell by 15 percent across the survey period. | The expansion of monitoring shows that predator numbers rose between 2018 and 2024.
explanation: A rate applied to a growing base can fall while the count it describes rises, and A works both readings: 22 percent of 100 nests is 22, and 15 percent of 400 is 60. B makes the opposite error, treating the falling percentage as a falling number. C reports the 2024 rate as though it were the change, which was 7 percentage points. D infers a cause the graph never measured from a change in monitoring effort.

question:
The editor of a quarterly poetry review describes a bar chart of the review's subscriber counts. Subscriptions climbed from 1,800 in 2005 to 4,200 in 2011, jumped to 9,000 in 2012 when the review absorbed the subscriber list of a closing rival, and eased down to 7,300 by 2015.

Which choice most effectively uses the chart to complete the editor's claim that the tallest bar overstates the review's own growth?
options: Subscriptions rose continuously from 2005 to 2015, which shows that the merger made no lasting difference. | The decline to 7,300 by 2015 shows that subscriptions fell below their 2005 level. | The peak of 9,000 rests on a one-off transfer of another publication's readers in 2012, since once that jump is set aside the review's own trajectory is rising only through 2011 and flat to falling thereafter. | The 2012 jump cannot be interpreted, because no data exist for the years around it.
explanation: Attributing a trend to the right years is the skill: the 2012 spike arrives with a documented event, and the series moves downward from 2012 to 2015, so the peak measures an acquisition rather than organic demand, as C explains. A ignores the post-2012 decline, and B miscompares endpoints, since 7,300 is far above 1,800. D claims a gap where the chart reports figures for each date discussed.

question:
A glaciology survey plots a valley glacier's terminus position against time, recording the distance retreated as a running total measured from the position the terminus held in 1850 rather than as the amount lost within each interval. The plotted values are 310 metres by 1990, 640 metres by 2010, and 1,050 metres by 2020.

Which choice most effectively uses the plotted figures to complete the survey's comparison of retreat rates across the three decades considered?
options: The glacier retreated 640 metres during the interval from 1990 to 2010. | Because the cumulative distance keeps growing, the rate of retreat declined after 2010. | In 2020 the terminus advanced 1,050 metres from where it had stood in 1850. | The glacier lost 410 metres of ice front between 2010 and 2020, against 330 metres across the twenty years to 1990, so the retreat was faster in the later decade.
explanation: Because the series is cumulative, only differences between plotted values measure activity in an interval, and D computes them: 410 metres in the last decade against 330 metres spread over two earlier ones, which is a genuine two-step rate comparison. A and C both hand an interval a cumulative figure, and C adds a reversal of direction by calling the change an advance. B confuses a growing total with a growing or shrinking rate.

question:
A national dietary survey describes an area chart showing how much of each respondent's daily added sugar came from sweetened drinks. The share fell from 34 percent in 2003 to 25 percent in 2023, while average daily added-sugar intake itself fell over the same years from 96 grams to 68 grams.

Which choice most effectively uses the chart to complete the survey's account of sugar consumed from drinks?
options: The 9-point fall in the share means that grams from drinks fell by 9 percent, from about 33 to about 30 grams per day. | Average daily intake from drinks went from roughly 33 grams to roughly 17 grams, a decline of about half that is sharper than the 9-point change in share suggests. | Because total intake fell, the intake from drinks must have risen. | Drinks remained the largest source of added sugar in 2023, since the share had fallen by only 9 points.
explanation: Two moving quantities require a multiplication the chart's labels do not perform: 34 percent of 96 grams is about 33 grams and 25 percent of 68 is about 17, so the decline in absolute intake far exceeds what the percentage-point shift implies. A treats a change in percentage points as though it were a percentage change in grams. C contradicts the figures by claiming a rise in a shrinking component of a shrinking total, and D ranks 2023 sources the survey does not compare.

question:
A productivity brief describes a chart of output per hour worked in three sectors of an economy, in dollars, for 2000 and 2022. Sector A moved from 58 dollars to 71 dollars; Sector B from 44 dollars to 46 dollars; Sector C from 30 dollars to 51 dollars.

Which choice most effectively uses the chart to complete the brief's comparison of growth in the three sectors between 2000 and 2022?
options: Sector B grew the most in proportional terms, since its figure rose by 2 dollars on the smallest base. | Sector C's gain of 21 percent is the largest in the chart, although Sector A remained the most productive sector in 2022. | Sector C's roughly 70 percent rise was the chart's steepest, and Sector B's rise of about 5 percent was the gentlest, yet both still trailed Sector A's 71 dollars per hour in 2022. | Sector A rose by about 22 dollars per hour, the largest increase in the chart.
explanation: Comparing growth across different starting levels requires percentages, which the chart's dollar figures do not supply: Sector C gained 21 dollars on a base of 30, about 70 percent, while Sector B gained 2 dollars on a base of 44, roughly 5 percent, and A's 71 dollars remained the highest level in 2022, as C states. A calls B's gain the largest in proportional terms and misnames 44 dollars the smallest base. B reports C's dollar gain as though it were a percentage. D miscomputes A's increase, which is 13 dollars.

question:
The Atacama Desert's soil holds almost no ____ in the hyperarid core have gone through entire years without logging a single millimeter of rain.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: moisture, weather stations | moisture; weather stations | moisture weather stations | moisture, where weather stations
explanation: Two independent clauses (the soil holds almost no moisture; weather stations have gone through entire years without rain) must be joined by something stronger than a bare comma, so the semicolon is right. A is a comma splice; C fuses the clauses into a run-on with no punctuation at all; D recasts the second clause as a relative clause on moisture, which leaves the sentence with no sensible main clause.

question:
Kiribati shifts the International Date Line eastward so that its scattered islands share a single calendar ____ crossing the line must still reset their logs.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: day; but vessels | day vessels | day, but vessels | day, vessels
explanation: Two independent clauses that contrast are correctly joined by a comma plus a coordinating conjunction: the islands share a single calendar day, but vessels crossing the line must still reset their logs. A puts a semicolon in front of but, where a semicolon may not introduce a coordinated clause; B fuses the clauses with no punctuation at all; D is a comma splice, since a comma alone cannot join the two clauses.

question:
Satin bowerbirds of southeastern Australia assemble twig towers on the forest floor for a single purpose: ____ the most ornamented bower usually courts the most females.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the claim that males compete for mates | males compete for mates, so | a competition among males for mates, so | males competing for mates, so
explanation: Whatever follows a colon that explains a complete clause must itself be able to stand alone as a sentence; only 'males compete for mates, so' supplies the verb compete as a main verb, giving 'males compete for mates, so the most ornamented bower usually courts the most females.' A and C insert the nouns claim and competition without a verb, producing a fragment after the colon; D demotes the verb to the participle competing, again leaving no independent clause.

question:
The canal network built by the Hohokam in today's Phoenix area ____ than 100 square kilometers of Sonoran desert, and archaeologists estimate that its longest canals ran for tens of kilometers.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: irrigated, more | irrigated more | irrigated; more | irrigated. More
explanation: Here the verb irrigated takes the direct object more than 100 square kilometers, and no punctuation may stand between a verb and its object. A and C drive a comma or a semicolon into the middle of that verb-object unit, so the first clause has no completed object; D's period cuts the object off entirely, leaving an incomplete first sentence and a fragment beginning More.

question:
The Helheim Glacier drains into a fjord in southeast ____ images from the same fjord show that its ice front retreated several kilometers between 1990 and 2020.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Greenland, satellite | Greenland; this satellite | Greenland. Satellite | Greenland satellite
explanation: Two complete thoughts, one about where the glacier drains and one about what the imagery shows, need a full stop between them, and only a period or a semicolon supplies one. A is a comma splice, since a bare comma cannot join two independent clauses; D fuses them with no punctuation at all; B is ungrammatical, because the singular this satellite cannot go with the plural images that follows it.

question:
The cluster of timber granaries raised on mushroom-shaped stone supports in the English ____ grain dry for centuries, and several of the structures still stand on farm grounds today.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: countryside kept | countryside, kept | countryside; kept | countryside. Kept
explanation: The subject is the single long phrase 'The cluster of timber granaries raised on mushroom-shaped stone supports in the English countryside,' and a subject may not be separated from its verb kept by any punctuation. B inserts a comma between subject and verb; C and D place a semicolon or a period there, which strands a subject with no predicate and turns what follows into a fragment.

question:
The Rosetta ____ granodiorite slab inscribed with three versions of a single decree, has stood in the British Museum in London since the year 1802.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Stone a | Stone, a | Stone; a | Stone: a
explanation: 'A granodiorite slab inscribed with three versions of a single decree' is a nonrestrictive appositive renaming the Rosetta Stone, so it must be opened by a comma and closed by one, and the closing comma is already printed after decree. A leaves the appositive fused to the subject with no punctuation; C and D try to place a semicolon or a colon where the sentence still has to run on to the verb has stood, which breaks the sentence into fragments.

question:
In the 1760s the Royal Navy began sheathing the underwater hulls of its warships with ____ fouling by marine organisms and allowed ships to stay at sea far longer than before.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: copper, which reduced | copper, which, reduced | copper; which reduced | copper which reduced
explanation: The relative pronoun which refers back to the whole preceding statement, so it introduces a nonrestrictive clause that must be opened with a comma: with copper, which reduced fouling... . B adds a second comma that drives a wedge between the relative subject which and its verb reduced; C puts a semicolon in front of a relative pronoun, which cannot begin an independent clause; D omits the comma a clause commenting on an entire earlier statement requires.

question:
Over four field seasons the survey team tagged 340 individual manta rays and recorded each animal's route through the shallow lagoon with small underwater ____ a task that took several crew members to complete.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: cameras, tags and loggers, | cameras, tags, and loggers | cameras, tags, and loggers; | cameras, tags, and loggers,
explanation: The series of three items needs its serial comma, and a comma must also close the list, because 'a task that took several crew members to complete' is a nonrestrictive appositive summarizing the whole undertaking. A drops the serial comma before and; B leaves the appositive fused onto the last noun with no comma at all; C's semicolon strands the appositive, which has no main verb of its own.

question:
Ash from the 79 CE eruption buried the seaside town of Oplontis in a single ____ wooden beams, painted plaster walls, and even loaves of bread were later recovered from the sealed layers.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: night; although | night, although | night: although | night. Although
explanation: The concessive clause beginning with although is dependent, so it must stay attached to the independent clause it concedes, which is exactly what a comma does. A's semicolon, C's colon and D's period each demand a complete sentence after them, yet what follows is an although clause with no main clause of its own, so all three turn the second half of the sentence into a fragment.

question:
The new sedative shortened recovery time after minor surgery; however, it also left a minority of patients drowsy well into the next ____ that surprised the trial's authors.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: morning, an effect | morning and an effect | morning an effect | morning; an effect
explanation: The noun effect stands in apposition to the whole preceding statement (drowsy well into the next morning, an effect that surprised the trial's authors), so it needs a comma in front of it and nothing else. B reaches for the conjunction and, but what follows is only a noun phrase, so there is no second clause to coordinate; C fuses the appositive onto the words it renames; D's semicolon strands the appositive as a fragment, since an effect that surprised the trial's authors has no main verb.

question:
The 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak is remembered less for the deaths it caused ____ for the investigative method John Snow used, which mapped cases pump by pump before germ theory was accepted.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: than, | more than | than | than;
explanation: The correlative pair less... than joins two parallel phrases (less for the deaths than for the method) and takes no punctuation at all. A drives a comma into the middle of the comparison; B's more contradicts the less already printed, so the sentence compares its two terms with mismatched degrees; D's semicolon cuts the second phrase away from the clause it depends on.

question:
The observatory's single 4.5-meter mirror gives it a wide ____ its fixed mounting means astronomers must wait for the sky to rotate into place rather than aim the telescope.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: view, however | view; however, | view, and however | view however
explanation: However is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so joining two independent clauses requires a semicolon before it and a comma after it: a wide view; however, its fixed mounting means... . A is a comma splice; C stacks and with however incoherently; D runs the clauses together with no punctuation.

question:
The 1908 event over the Stony Tunguska River basin in Siberia ____ forests for more than 2,000 square kilometers, even though no impact crater has ever been found there.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: flattening | which flattened | it flattened | flattened
explanation: The sentence needs a main verb for its subject (the 1908 event), and flattened supplies it: the event flattened forests..., even though... . A's participle leaves the sentence with no finite verb; B buries everything in a relative clause, so nothing is ever asserted; C creates a splice, with 'the event' left dangling in front of a new clause.

question:
Because the reading rooms of the Bibliothèque nationale de France were crowded out of the Latin Quarter in 1997, its architects ____ tall glass-walled rooms in the new building.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: having designed | designed, | designed | designing
explanation: A because clause is dependent, so the sentence still needs an independent clause with a finite verb, and 'its architects designed tall glass-walled rooms in the new building' is exactly that. A's having designed makes the clause absolute instead of finite, so the whole sentence never reaches a main verb; B drives a comma between designed and its object; D's participle designing leaves no finite main verb at all.

question:
Although the small colony of California sea otters has rebounded from the brink of extinction, ____ along parts of the coast.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: keeping the numbers of sea urchins in check | the otters' keeping of sea urchins in check | which keeps sea urchin numbers in check | their predation keeps sea urchin numbers in check
explanation: An although clause is dependent, so what follows the comma has to be a complete independent clause, and 'their predation keeps sea urchin numbers in check along parts of the coast' is one, with their pointing back to the sea otters. A's participle keeping and B's gerund phrase the otters' keeping of leave the sentence with no main verb; C buries the verb inside a which clause, so the colony is never said to do anything.

question:
When the great ice sheets of the last glacial period ____ over northern Europe, they scraped deep basins into the bedrock that the meltwater later filled.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: advanced slowly | advancing slowly | slow advance | their slow advance
explanation: The when clause needs a finite verb of its own before the independent clause (they scraped deep basins) can follow, so 'advanced slowly' is correct. B's participle and C's noun advance leave the opening clause without a verb, making the whole sentence a fragment; D turns the clause's subject into a possessive phrase, again with no verb, so the when clause never resolves.

question:
A study of 14 metropolitan systems found that average fares had covered barely half of operating costs for decades, and that this gap ____ in transit ridership after commuters turned to private cars.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: widening the decline | it widened the decline | widened the decline | which widened the decline
explanation: The second half of the found that construction needs a finite verb of its own, so 'that this gap widened the decline in transit ridership after commuters turned to private cars' is the only complete version. A's participle widening and D's relative clause which widened both leave that clause without a main verb, creating a fragment; B piles a second subject (it) onto the subject this gap, a run-on.

question:
The linguist who compiled the first grammar of an unwritten language in the region often worked from a single fluent speaker, and the recordings that her fieldwork ____ among the primary evidence used by later analysts.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: yielded | yielded, are | have yielded | are yielding
explanation: The subject of the second clause is 'the recordings that her fieldwork yielded,' which needs the main verb are to go with the complement among the primary evidence; yielded must stay the past-tense verb inside the relative clause. B's comma separates the subject recordings from its verb are; C and D move are into the relative clause, so the outer sentence is left with no finite verb at all.

question:
The first telescopes able to detect infrared radiation from the ground were built in the 1960s, and because the atmosphere absorbs most such wavelengths, ____ high, dry mountaintops.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the siting of infrared observatories on | siting infrared observatories on | infrared observatories, were sited on | infrared observatories were sited on
explanation: The because clause is dependent, so the sentence needs a main clause of its own with a subject and a finite verb, and 'infrared observatories were sited on high, dry mountaintops' supplies both. A uses the noun siting and B the participle siting, so the sentence closes with no main verb at all; C sets a comma between the subject observatories and its verb were sited.

question:
So many households in the district signed the new water contract in its first month that the utility ____ an extra shift at the pumping station.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: and scheduling | it scheduled | scheduling | had to schedule
explanation: A so... that construction needs a finite verb inside the that clause, and 'the utility had to schedule an extra shift at the pumping station' provides it. A's and scheduling adds a conjunction with no finite verb, leaving the clause unfinished; B stacks a second subject, it, onto the subject the utility, a run-on; C's bare participle scheduling likewise gives the clause no main verb.

question:
In the 1920s a team of folklorists began interviewing mill workers in Connecticut, and the wax cylinders they recorded ____ what the company payroll ledgers do not: the reasons the workers themselves gave for leaving the job.
